Following Donald Trump's election as US President, the global economy faces heightened uncertainty. Following the inauguration of the new US administration, the direction of US policy could undergo fundamental shifts in two areas: from monetary easing to fiscal expansion, and from globalization to deglobalization—changes that may have profound implications for the global economic landscape. Notably, the risks faced by emerging market economies have intensified given the accelerated pace of US interest rate hikes, the strengthening of the US dollar, and the possibility of the US adopting trade protectionist measures. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained broadly stable, while the Hong Kong dollar interbank offer rates rose in line with U.S. dollar interbank rates. Nevertheless, liquidity conditions remained sound, and overall loan growth further increased in the second half of 2016. Following the implementation of the new stamp duty measures, the residential property market initially showed signs of adjustment but has recently picked up. Looking ahead, banks should prudently assess the possibility that the pace of US interest rate hikes may exceed expectations, as well as the broader impact of US policy uncertainty, particularly the risk of significant capital outflows and their potential implications for local interest rates. Following Donald Trump's election as US President, the global economy faces heightened uncertainty. Not only did the election results catch the market off guard, but the ensuing market reaction also proved surprisingly unexpected. In particular, expectations that President Trump's tax reform, increased infrastructure spending, and regulatory deregulation would boost US economic growth drove a rally in global equity markets. After the new US administration took office, US policy direction could undergo fundamental shifts in two areas — from monetary easing to fiscal expansion, and from globalization to deglobalization — which may have profound implications for the global economic landscape. However, the tax cuts under Trump that markets had anticipated may fail to deliver the expected boost to US economic growth. In particular, with US economic activity already close to its potential, fiscal stimulus is likely to provide only a modest cyclical boost to US growth while heightening upside risks to US inflation. While it remains uncertain whether the Federal Reserve will significantly accelerate the pace of monetary tightening as a result, long-term bond yields have risen markedly, partly reflecting market expectations of increasing inflation risks. Meanwhile, the rise of trade protectionism would result in a "lose-lose" outcome for the United States and other regions around the world. Increased trade barriers can distort markets, undermine overall welfare, hinder global trade flows, reduce the efficiency of global supply chains, and pose downside risks to the global economic outlook. At the same time, political instability remains a key risk and a headwind, particularly for Europe's still-fragile recovery. For emerging market economies, the risk of capital outflows driven by an acceleration in the pace of US interest rate hikes and further appreciation of the US dollar has increased. This could dampen economic growth and exacerbate the risk of rapid capital outflows. In fact, amid expectations of expansive fiscal policies under the Trump administration and concerns over a sharp surge in energy prices, markets have repriced inflation risks, leading to a broad and significant rise in long-term bond yields across advanced economies and numerous emerging market economies. Topic 1 (see page 13): Assessing the potential spillover effects of US rate hike expectations on the sovereign bond markets of 26 selected economies. The findings indicate that since the 2013 "taper tantrum," the impact of the US Treasury market on sovereign bond markets has deepened, and US interest rate hikes and tightening financial conditions have had significant effects on both advanced economies and emerging market economies. In East Asia, economic growth picked up slightly in the second half of 2016 as exports rebounded, but market volatility—including currency depreciation and rising sovereign bond yields in the region triggered by concerns over potential policy shifts by the incoming U.S. administration—only gradually subsided by the beginning of this year. Looking ahead, East Asia may sustain stable growth in 2017, though risks and uncertainties are rising. US interest rate hikes, regional currency depreciation, and heightened financial market volatility could collectively lead to tighter financial conditions. At the same time, the United States may pursue protectionist policies, which could impact regional economies, although the actual effects remain uncertain at present. In Mainland China, the overall economic growth picked up slightly in the second half of 2016, supported by robust growth in infrastructure investment and an improvement in private sector business spending. Although there are continued signs of economic stabilisation, the growth outlook in mainland China remains uncertain. Especially in light of the government's resolve to curb rising housing prices, if the real estate market continues to cool, the sector's contribution to economic growth this year may diminish. At the same time, the ongoing structural economic adjustments and shifts in China-US trade relations may heighten uncertainty in the near-term economic outlook. Externally, although the renminbi remained stable against a basket of currencies of the China Foreign Exchange Trade System (CFETS) during the reporting period, capital outflow pressures increased by the end of 2016 amid a strengthening US dollar and US interest rate hikes, before easing somewhat in early 2017. Although there are signs of stabilization in private-sector economic activity, concerns persist regarding the effectiveness of monetary policy, particularly given the acceleration in M1 growth alongside a slowdown in M2 growth. Special Feature 2 (see page 24) examines whether China's economy is falling into a liquidity trap, while Special Feature 3 (see page 27) explores the factors that may lead to a divergence between M1 and M2 growth. The findings indicate no evidence that mainland China has fallen into a liquidity trap. The fact that M1 growth has significantly outpaced M2 growth is primarily attributable to the reduced opportunity cost of holding liquid money due to recent monetary easing, alongside potentially heightened demand for precautionary money amid rising economic uncertainty. Hong Kong's economic growth accelerated slightly in the second half of 2016. Quarter-on-quarter real GDP growth rose from 0.8% in the third quarter to 1.2% in the fourth quarter. Domestically, private consumption growth continued to strengthen, while robust infrastructure activity in the fourth quarter boosted investment growth. On the external front, goods export growth rose alongside improved intra-regional trade flows, while services exports expanded steadily, supported by the recovery in trade-related and transport services. Due to the faster growth in goods and services imports, net trade continued to drag on real GDP growth in the second half of the year. As economic growth rose, the headline unemployment rate dipped slightly to 3.3% in December. Economic growth in 2017 is expected to remain moderate. The Government and the market consensus forecast real GDP growth for 2017 at 2–3% and 2.0%, respectively. However, Hong Kong's growth outlook continues to face significant headwinds from external sources. The protectionist rhetoric of the new US administration has heightened downside risks for global trade and Hong Kong's external demand. Against a backdrop of dollar appreciation pressure and expectations of an accelerated pace of US rate hikes, the global financial environment is likely to provide diminished support to the real economy, particularly with the potential for tighter local financial conditions should tail risks materialize. Topic 4 (see page 41) discusses the construction of the Hong Kong Financial Conditions Index to help monitor local financial conditions. Since the second half of 2016, local inflation pressures have remained mild, with quarterly inflationary momentum accelerating slightly in the fourth quarter of 2016, primarily due to fluctuations in food prices and rising housing rentals. With stable import prices and moderate domestic cost pressures, inflation is expected to remain under control. Despite market volatility, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained broadly stable, although it occasionally weakened following the US interest rate hike in December. The Convertibility Undertakings have not been triggered. As the US dollar appreciated, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate rose further. Due to the large size of the monetary base, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBOR) remained low, but have risen since October amid year-end funding needs and the catch-up to US interest rate hikes. Therefore, after falling to a recent low of 1.71% in October amid fierce competition in the mortgage lending market, the average mortgage rate rose slightly to 2.07% in January 2017. Overall loan growth accelerated to 4.2% in the second half of 2016, compared to 2.2% in the first half. The growth was supported by stronger local economic activity and heightened year-end financing demand from multinational corporations. Domestic loans experienced a slight acceleration in growth, while loans for use outside Hong Kong, which had seen a modest decline in the first half, rebounded. By currency, HKD loans recorded robust growth of 5.0% in the second half of the year, while foreign currency loans grew by 3.2% as mainland borrowers gradually reduced their repayment of foreign currency loans. Banking funding positions remained broadly sound. The HKD loan-to-deposit ratio fell slightly to 77.1% at the end of 2016, reflecting that deposit growth exceeded loan growth. The overall foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio fell to 59.9% by year-end, while the US dollar loan-to-deposit ratio dropped significantly to 63.8%, driven by robust growth in US dollar deposits. Due to the strong US dollar, both onshore and offshore RMB exchange rates weakened. Against this backdrop, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi (CNH) liquidity pool (comprising customer deposits and certificates of deposit) further consolidated relative to other offshore renminbi markets, while volatility in the overnight and three-month CNH HIBOR increased markedly. Notwithstanding this, the banks' RMB liquidity management remained sound, and the average daily transaction value of the RMB Real-Time Gross Settlement System continued to stay at a high level. The Hong Kong offshore renminbi business is likely to continue facing headwinds from the uncertainty surrounding the renminbi exchange rate trend. Amid improving global market conditions, the Hong Kong equity market closed substantially higher during the reporting period. Although the US presidential election yielded an unexpected outcome, the market experienced only a brief shock. This was primarily due to investors' optimism regarding the fiscal stimulus measures of the Trump administration, which propelled the rise in global equity markets. While benefiting from this, the Hong Kong market, despite its optimism, remains cautious, likely due to concerns over an accelerated pace of US rate hikes, challenges facing the mainland's economic outlook, uncertainties in RMB-related policies, and capital flow controls. Looking ahead, although the local market may be affected by external economic conditions, its attractive valuations are expected to provide support. Although Hong Kong dollar bond yields surged sharply towards the end of last year, widening rapidly against US Treasury yields, the Hong Kong dollar bond market continued to expand steadily during the reporting period. Meanwhile, the offshore renminbi bond market in Hong Kong contracted in the first half of 2016 but recovered in the second half, although total new bond issuance for the year remained lower than the previous year. Looking ahead, if global investors reverse their earlier yield-seeking investment strategies, both the Hong Kong dollar and offshore renminbi bond markets could come under pressure. Given the ongoing uncertainty surrounding US trade policies, the renminbi exchange rate may continue to experience volatility, and the outlook for these two bond markets over the next six months remains heavily clouded by significant uncertainties. Following the introduction of new stamp duty measures by the government, the residential property market showed signs of adjustment, but has recently picked up. Given the market's renewed exuberance, the government raised the stamp duty to a uniform 15% in November. Transaction volumes in both the primary and secondary markets declined in the following two months. However, transaction volume has recently increased, partly reflecting developers' efforts to launch more new residential projects. Meanwhile, property prices continued to rise to new highs, though the pace of increase has moderated.

Following Trump's unexpected election as US President, uncertainty in US policy has increased. While market focus remains on the short-term benefits of potentially implemented large-scale fiscal policies and business-friendly measures, US economic activity is already near its potential. Fiscal stimulus is likely to provide only a modest cyclical boost to US growth, while further elevating upside risks to inflation. More importantly, the risks facing emerging market economies are escalating due to capital outflow pressures driven by the pace of US interest rate hikes and a strengthening US dollar, while the potential adoption of US trade protectionist measures poses a threat to global trade flows. In East Asia, real economic activity improved slightly in the second half of 2016, with export volumes also rising recently. However, amid US rate hikes, a strengthening US dollar, and the possibility of protectionist measures by the United States, financial markets are likely to remain volatile, with downside risks to economic growth increasing. In Mainland China, the overall economic growth picked up slightly in the second half of 2016, supported by robust growth in infrastructure investment and an improvement in private sector business spending. The mainland economy continues to undergo rebalancing, with the tertiary sector expanding steadily; however, the ongoing structural adjustment and changes in China-US trade relations may heighten uncertainty in the near-term economic outlook. Amid the government's resolve to curb housing price increases, if the real estate market continues to cool, the sector's contribution to economic growth this year may also diminish. Externally, although the renminbi remained stable against a basket of currencies in the China Foreign Exchange Trade System (CFETS) during the reporting period, capital outflow pressures increased towards the end of 2016 amid a stronger US dollar and US interest rate hikes, before easing slightly in early 2017. Following Donald Trump's unexpected election as US President, global financial markets reacted strongly, particularly as investors anticipated that his policies—such as tax reform, large-scale infrastructure spending, and regulatory easing—would boost US economic growth and inflation, thereby propelling major stock markets higher (Figure 2.1). Consequently, heightened market expectations regarding US inflation and further US interest rate hikes have driven a sharp rise in US Treasury yields and strengthened the US dollar. Chart 2.1 Equity market indices in select advanced economies However, the tax cuts by Trump that markets had anticipated may fail to deliver the positive impact on US economic growth that was expected. While a shift in economic policy toward fiscal expansion could help alleviate the heavy burden on monetary easing, whether the current timing is appropriate for implementing fiscal expansion remains debatable given the present stage of the US economic cycle. Although the pace of US economic growth has moderated in recent quarters, the output gap has gradually narrowed, and the February unemployment rate aligned with the Federal Reserve's estimate of a 4.7% natural rate, indicating that US economic activity is approaching its potential. The US economy is currently in an expansionary phase, during which the fiscal multiplier is expected to be lower than during a recession (see, for example, Auerbach and Gorodnichenko, 2012). In fact, recent estimates of the US Laffer curve suggest that tax cuts on labor or capital may lead to a reduction in tax revenues (see, for example, Trabandt and Uhlig, 2012)². In any event, with excess capacity diminishing, any further measures aimed at boosting economic growth, even if their substantive impact on growth is limited, could nonetheless drive up inflation. At the same time, other factors, including rising oil and commodity prices and potential trade protectionist measures such as the Border Adjustment Tax currently under consideration, may further exacerbate the upside risks to US inflation. Even as the risks of rising inflation in the United States increase, the Federal Reserve remains cautious about tightening U.S. monetary policy and continues to favor maintaining an ultra-loose monetary policy stance. However, long-term bond yields have risen, partly reflecting increased inflation risks in the United States. Since the U.S. election, although market expectations for future federal funds rates have risen to near the median of the Federal Reserve's projections for early 2017 and 2018, they remain well below the Fed's long-term projections (Chart 2.2). Therefore, an accelerated pace of US rate hikes may trigger the risk of significant market volatility. While the focus of financial markets is on the short-term benefits of potential expansionary fiscal policies and business-friendly measures that could drive stronger US economic growth, long-term risks remain, including damaging protectionist trade policies and further rises in US government debt. In fact, the Trump administration may fulfill its election promises by adopting protectionist trade measures. Rising trade barriers are likely to distort markets, undermine overall welfare, impede global trade, reduce the efficiency of global supply chains, and pose downside risks to the global economic outlook. Chart 2.2 Future Fed Funds Rate Forecasts: Federal Reserve vs. Markets In Europe, political instability remains a key risk and impediment to economic recovery. Although the economic environment in the euro area has gradually improved, with real GDP recording a modest 1.7% year-on-year growth in the fourth quarter—only slightly below the 1.8% expansion in the third quarter—economic activity remains just above pre-global financial crisis levels when compared to the stronger recovery in the United States (Chart 2.3). Since the UK's decision to leave the EU last summer, markets have remained concerned about the potential disintegration of the eurozone. Although Italy's economic and political situation appears to have stabilized following the formation of a new government and the implementation of measures to safeguard the banking sector, upcoming elections in Germany and France—and potentially Italy—could become flashpoints for political instability against the backdrop of Brexit negotiations and rising anti-establishment sentiment. Partly due to rising political uncertainty, sovereign bond yields in Europe have continued to climb, while corporate bond spreads have widened, a trend particularly pronounced in peripheral countries. This could trigger a vicious cycle for the real economy and place pressure on business real investment in the euro area. Chart 2.3 Real GDP Growth in Major Advanced Economies  In Japan, real GDP has been revised upward in recent quarters, with the year-on-year growth rate reaching 1.6% in the fourth quarter of 2016, the fastest pace since the third quarter of 2015, indicating a stronger-than-expected economic recovery. However, structural issues in the labour market have contributed to sluggish wage growth, which in turn has led to weak consumption growth. At the same time, the recent sharp depreciation of the Japanese yen suggests that the downward pressure exerted by the earlier yen appreciation on "new core" goods inflation is about to begin easing. With recovery momentum proving stronger than expected, the near-term inflation outlook has improved. Meanwhile, "new core" inflation (excluding fresh food and energy), although dipping to 0.1% in December, is expected to have bottomed out and is poised to rebound. Nevertheless, amid persistent headwinds from long-term and structural factors, growth may remain sluggish, and inflation expectations could stay in the range of 0.5%–0.6%, below the level at the time the Abenomics policy was launched in early 2014. Consequently, the risk of inflation failing to meet the Bank of Japan's medium-term target of 2% remains. For other countries, particularly emerging market economies, the benefits of faster US economic growth transmitted through trade channels may be limited, given the decline in US imports following the global financial crisis and the possibility of the United States adopting protectionist policies. At the same time, the accelerated pace of US rate hikes and further appreciation of the US dollar will tighten financial conditions, thereby heightening the risks of an economic downturn. This could weigh on economic growth and heighten the risk of a rapid outflow of capital. Indeed, market expectations of expansive fiscal policies under the Trump administration, coupled with concerns over a sharp rise in energy prices, have prompted a repricing of inflation risks, leading to a broad and significant increase in long-term bond yields across advanced economies and numerous emerging market economies. Topic 1 assesses the potential spillover effects of US interest rate hike expectations on sovereign bond markets in 26 selected economies. In East Asia, economic activity has recently regained momentum, with regional GDP registering modest growth and inflation rising. Real GDP Growth – In the second half of 2016, with private consumption in several regional economies remaining steady, economic growth was generally stable. At the same time, exports rose modestly across the board from their 2015 lows. This was supported not only by China's economic growth stabilizing but also by improved performance in advanced economies such as the United States and Europe. For net commodity exporters such as Malaysia and Indonesia, the rebound in commodity prices also provided an additional boost. Other major exporting economies, such as the Republic of Korea, Taiwan, and Singapore, have also regained momentum, driven by growth in electronics and semiconductor exports. Inflation — As commodity prices (especially oil) have risen, producer price inflation has broadly trended upward. Although this may raise industrial costs and even consumption expenditures, consumption and investment growth could potentially increase as the risk of prolonged deflation diminishes. Accelerating producer price inflation may exert upward pressure on consumer price inflation; the actual impact will depend on the extent to which producer price increases are passed through to consumer prices, a process that varies across economies. Consensus forecasts for the consumer price index indicate that while inflation in several regional economies will remain slightly below the 2% inflation targets set by their respective central banks in 2017, it is expected to rise toward levels closer to those targets (Chart 2.4). With the exception of Indonesia, central banks across East Asia generally maintained their accommodative monetary policy stance unchanged, while Indonesia implemented two rate cuts in September and October of last year to stimulate growth. Chart 2.4 East Asia: Headline CPI Inflation, Forecasts, and Central Bank Targets Although the real economy has improved, the outcome of the November 2016 U.S. presidential election was unexpected, triggering short-term volatility in financial markets. Foreign Exchange Markets — Following the US presidential election, investors' expectations of higher US inflation led to depreciation of most currencies in the region against the US dollar. However, on a trade-weighted basis, some regional currencies have depreciated by a smaller margin or even appreciated slightly since the US election (Chart 2.5). Chart 2.5 Post-U.S. Election Spot Exchange Rate Depreciation Against the U.S. Dollar and Movements in the Nominal Effective Exchange Rate Bond and Equity Markets — Asset prices briefly declined following the U.S. presidential election but subsequently stabilized. The spread between sovereign bond yields in East Asian economies and U.S. Treasury bond yields has widened. However, following the stabilization of markets, yields in some regional economies declined, though they have not yet returned to pre-election levels. (Figure 2.6). Nevertheless, the interest margin has narrowed compared to pre-election levels. Figure 2.6: Spread between 10-year sovereign bonds and US Treasury bonds, and securities investment flows. Securities investment funds exited East Asia in the fourth quarter of 2016, but at a slower pace than during the "taper tantrum" in mid-2013. In the first few weeks of 2017, capital inflows resumed, supporting asset prices and financial conditions. Looking ahead, growth in the region is expected to remain stable, albeit at a pace below historical averages. Given the rising uncertainties surrounding US government policies and potential Federal Reserve policy responses, financial markets are likely to remain volatile. A significant rise in the US dollar and interest rates could attract capital outflows from the region to the United States, prompting investors to reduce their holdings of regional assets, with particular concern for those assets that are already valued at elevated levels. Tighter financial conditions in this scenario would also place repayment pressures on firms with substantial USD-denominated debt. Macroecologically, widespread global interest rate hikes will also reduce fixed capital investment in the region, which not only drags down aggregate demand in the short term but may also affect potential growth in the long term. Finally, exporting economies in the region face the potential threat of the new US administration's implementation of protectionist trade policies. The trade deficit between the United States and East Asian economies has continued to widen in recent years (Figure 2.7), particularly in the region's key export sectors such as electronics, electrical appliances, automobiles, apparel, and textiles. Over the past two decades, U.S. imports in these sectors have increased, leading to significant job losses. Protectionist policies aimed at reducing the trade deficit and revitalizing US manufacturing could pose significant risks to export-oriented economies within the region.

Accelerated growth in private consumption and robust public sector building and construction activities propelled a slight acceleration in Hong Kong's economic growth during the second half of 2016. Given the increasingly uncertain external environment, economic growth in 2017 is expected to be modest. Supported by stable import prices and moderate domestic growth momentum, inflation pressures are expected to remain contained. Hong Kong's economic growth accelerated slightly in the second half of 2016. On a seasonally adjusted quarter-on-quarter basis, real GDP grew by 1.2% in the fourth quarter, slightly higher than the 0.8% growth recorded in the third quarter (Chart 3.1). Partly due to improved consumer confidence and a robust labour market, the pace of private consumption growth accelerated, becoming the main driver of GDP growth. Supported by infrastructure projects such as the third runway at Hong Kong International Airport, building and construction activities have also gained significant momentum. However, weak corporate capital expenditure narrowed the contribution of total investment spending to GDP growth. On the external front, both imports and exports accelerated in line with rising intra-regional trade flows (Figure 3.2). Trade-related and transport services further propelled the growth in exports of services, while imports of services rebounded partly due to strong travel demand from local residents. Net exports continued to drag on GDP growth. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth rate and contribution by major expenditure components; Chart 3.2 Real imports and exports; The labor market remains tight. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate remained at 3.4% during the first three quarters and then declined slightly to 3.3% in the fourth quarter (Chart 3.3). In fact, unemployment rates in several major industries declined in the second half of the year, including retail, accommodation, and food services, partly due to a stabilization in the slowdown of the retail sector. Total employment reached a record high of 3.824 million in February 2017, while the labour force participation rate remained steady at approximately 61%. Chart 3.3 Unemployment rate and total employment; Real economic growth is expected to remain moderate in 2017. On the external front, given the uncertainties in the global macroeconomic and financial environment, global economic and trade growth is likely to remain moderate. Furthermore, the strength of the US dollar has led to an appreciation of the Hong Kong dollar's real effective exchange rate, which will dampen Hong Kong's export performance. On the domestic front, while stable employment and income conditions are expected to support consumption, rising interest rates are likely to dampen private consumption, leading to only moderate growth. With an increase in housing supply and the commencement of several infrastructure projects, building and construction activities are expected to grow steadily, although subdued business sentiment and rising interest rates may dampen corporate capital expenditure. The Government currently forecasts real GDP growth for 2017 in the range of 2% to 3%, while private-sector analysts' average forecast is 2.0%. The economic growth outlook is constrained by numerous uncertainties, with external factors posing particularly significant challenges. Policy uncertainty under the new US administration will cloud the global economic outlook, and the potential emergence of trade protectionist measures could impede global trade flows. The Brexit process and upcoming general elections in several major European countries may also trigger volatility in asset markets and affect the flow of Hong Kong dollar funds. Furthermore, the normalization of US interest rates will tighten local monetary conditions and exert downward pressure on the real economy and asset prices. Since the second half of 2016, although local inflation has gained quarterly momentum in recent months, it has remained moderate overall. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying composite consumer price index remained stable at 2.1% from the second half of 2016 through January this year (Chart 3.4). The annualised three-month-on-three-month underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflationary momentum, accelerated from 0.9% in the third quarter to 3.0% in the fourth quarter, before dipping slightly to 2.4% in January. The main drivers of rising inflationary pressures have been increases in the prices of traded goods and housing rentals (Figure 3.5). Inflation in tradeable goods prices rose from negative in the third quarter to 3.0% in the fourth quarter, mainly driven by prices of basic food items and clothing and footwear. Meanwhile, since the third quarter, the housing rental component of the CCPI rose as the decline in private residential rentals narrowed and public rental housing rents were increased in September 2016, though the pace of increase moderated slightly in January (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.4 Different measures of consumer price inflation Chart 3.5 Consumer price inflation by major components Chart 3.6 Rental component of the composite consumer price index and market rents In the short term, given weak import prices and moderate domestic cost pressures, inflation is expected to remain under control. Due to the strong performance of the Hong Kong dollar, which partially offset the rebound in global commodity prices, imported inflation remained subdued (Figure 3.7). At the local level, the output gap was estimated to be close to zero in the fourth quarter of 2016, which should have helped alleviate business cost pressures and thereby contain inflation in the services component. Despite the tight labour market, wage growth remained modest in recent quarters; real per capita earnings rose by 1.1% in the first half of 2016, before falling by 0.4% in the third quarter (Chart 3.8). Given the persistent uncertainty in the external environment, which has fostered a cautious business sentiment, wage cost increases are expected to be restrained under these circumstances. Furthermore, given the weak retail sales performance over recent months, the growth in retail property rents is expected to be modest. Furthermore, the earlier moderation in private residential rents will gradually come into play, helping to alleviate inflationary pressures. Overall, the annual inflation rate for 2017 is expected to decline; the Government forecasts underlying inflation for the full year at 2.0%, down from 2.3% in 2016. Chart 3.7 Goods and import prices Chart 3.8 Unit labour cost and real wage per capita Inflation outlook faces both upside and downside risks. On the downside, if inflation accelerates more rapidly under the Trump administration, it could lead to a faster-than-expected pace of US interest rate hikes, potentially pushing up local mortgage rates and increasing downward pressure on property prices and rental levels. At the same time, the appreciation of the Hong Kong dollar could further weaken import prices while simultaneously reducing the attractiveness of Hong Kong to visiting tourists. On the upside, if the global economy expands faster than expected, Hong Kong's economic growth could accelerate, pushing up demand-driven international commodity prices and thereby exerting upward pressure on local inflation. Furthermore, the statutory minimum wage, having been raised, will take effect on May 1, 2017, which may lead to further inflation; however, the actual impact of this cost-push inflation will depend on the extent to which higher wage costs are passed through to consumer prices.

Despite volatility in financial markets, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained broadly stable, while the Hong Kong dollar interbank lending rate rose in line with the US dollar interbank rate. Partly due to an improved local economic environment, overall loans continued to grow moderately. Looking ahead, fund-flow volatility for the Hong Kong dollar could increase as the pace of US interest rate normalization accelerates, the policy direction of the incoming US administration remains uncertain, and political risks persist in Europe. Despite volatility in financial markets, the spot exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar against the US dollar remained broadly stable (Chart 4.1). Although market volatility triggered by the November US presidential election led to a broad decline in Asian currencies, the Hong Kong dollar's spot exchange rate against the US dollar remained stable. However, the interest rate projections released by the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) at its meeting on December 13–14, 2016, heightened market expectations for an accelerated pace of US rate hikes, leading to a brief weakening of the Hong Kong dollar in the subsequent period. In early 2017, the Hong Kong dollar strengthened alongside other Asian currencies; however, as market expectations of a U.S. interest rate hike in March rose from mid-February, signs of weakness began to emerge in the Hong Kong dollar. During the reporting period, the Convertibility Undertakings were not triggered (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Exchange Rate and Capital Flow Indicators Chart 4.2 Capital Flow Indicators Following the strength of the US dollar, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index rose by 4.9% between August and December before stabilising in recent months (Chart 4.3). Due to the limited impact of the narrowing inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index closely tracked the movement of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.3 Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rates Portfolio investment saw outflows in the second half of 2016. Latest balance of payments statistics indicate a net inflow of foreign investment in Hong Kong's equity and debt securities in the third quarter, reflecting improved global market sentiment and a wave of initial public offerings (Table 4.A). However, driven by local banks' increased holdings of US bonds, net outflows from debt investments by local residents were substantial, outweighing the inflows from non-resident investors. Consequently, cross-border securities investment registered net outflows in the third quarter. A survey of global mutual funds revealed net outflows from securities investments in the final quarter of 2016, primarily driven by the unexpected outcome of the U.S. presidential election and expectations of an accelerated pace of U.S. rate hikes, which placed downward pressure on local financial markets and other Asian markets (Figure 4.4). However, the latest data indicate that Hong Kong's securities investment experienced net capital inflows in the first quarter of 2017, partly due to investors' optimism regarding the United States' adoption of expansionary fiscal policies, which led to an improvement in global financial markets. Chart 4.4 Market Survey on Stock and Bond-related Fund Flows Looking ahead, volatility in Hong Kong dollar fund flows may increase. An acceleration in the pace of US interest rate normalization would increase the risk of a reversal in Hong Kong dollar capital flows. At the same time, with uncertainties surrounding the new US administration, the Brexit process, and elections in EU member states, capital flows could become more volatile. Additionally, the rising investment demand from mainland investors for Hong Kong dollar-denominated assets could exert upward pressure on the Hong Kong dollar through capital inflows. Although the initial trading volume northbound via the Stock Connect exceeded southbound flows shortly after its launch in December, it is expected that two-way stock investment capital flows between mainland China and Hong Kong under the scheme will gradually increase. Despite the rise in U.S. interest rates and financial market volatility, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2016 and in recent months. The Hong Kong monetary base remained large and rose further by 1.7% in the second half of the year, driven by increases in liability certificates and government-issued banknotes and coins in circulation (Chart 4.5). As the currency peg was not triggered, the aggregate balance remained broadly stable at a high level of HK$1,222.7 billion, corresponding to the total outstanding amount of Exchange Fund Bills and Bonds. In particular, the issuance of an additional HK$49 billion of Exchange Fund Bills and Bonds to meet banks' substantial liquidity management needs led to a contraction in total balances, while outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Bonds increased correspondingly. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base With the local economy gradually becoming more resilient, the pace of growth in the Hong Kong dollar money supply has accelerated. The growth rate of Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (HKD M3) accelerated from 2.3% in the first half of the year to 6.5% in the second half. As a major component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits registered a robust 6.6% growth in the second half of the year (Chart 4.7), driven primarily by heightened local economic activity and a resurgence in initial public offering activities, which boosted transaction demand. By asset analysis, the growth in M3 (HKD) mainly reflected increases in HKD loans and the banking sector's net foreign currency assets (Chart 4.6), which in turn reflected monetary expansion and net inflows of HKD funds into the non-bank private sector. Figure 4.6 Movements in HKD M3 and Corresponding Assets On the other hand, growth in foreign currency deposits continued to vary across categories. After a 10.2% increase in the first half of the year, USD deposits rose by a higher 12.8% in the second half amid a strong US dollar (Chart 4.7). In contrast, other foreign currency deposits contracted further by 10.3%, primarily due to a decline in RMB deposits. Due to the appreciation of the US dollar, both offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates weakened (Chart 4.14). As markets reassessed US inflation risks, global financial markets witnessed renewed volatility at the start of the year. In February, global equity markets plunged sharply from their highs at the end of January, erasing the significant gains recorded at the start of the year, while the benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury yield rose to a four-year high. Over the past two years, global equity markets have continued to rise amid low volatility, driven by market expectations of sustained robust economic growth, alongside persistently low inflation and interest rates. However, this expectation faces risks from tightening global monetary conditions, rising sentiment towards trade protectionism, and heightened geopolitical tensions. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened, while the market continued to operate in an orderly manner. In the second half of 2017, overall lending continued to grow, albeit at a slower pace. After a modest slowdown in the previous year, both the pace of house price increases and transaction volumes rebounded in the fourth quarter of 2017. Looking ahead, renewed volatility in global and local financial markets could add further volatility to capital flows into and out of Hong Kong. Given the uncertainties in financial markets, alongside the ongoing normalization of U.S. monetary policy and persistent geopolitical risks, banks should remain vigilant against heightened interest rate volatility and potential capital outflows. In particular, given that corporate leverage continues to rise and household debt remains elevated, banks should assess the potential impact of interest rate increases exceeding expectations on asset quality. After the Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index (VIX) remained at low levels for more than the past two years, global financial markets experienced renewed volatility at the beginning of the year. Global equity markets declined sharply from their late January highs, with the S&P 500 falling more than 10% at one point, completely erasing the significant gains recorded in early January. Market sentiment has shifted amid signs that a global economic recovery could exert pressure on US wages and prices, which have remained subdued for an extended period, potentially prompting the Federal Reserve to accelerate its rate-hiking pace. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high. Over the past two years, global equity markets have enjoyed a sustained upward trend, underpinned by market expectations of continued favorable economic conditions. In the second half of 2017, global economic growth momentum continued to strengthen, with economic activity rebounding synchronously across both advanced and emerging market economies. As year-end approached, the US Congress passed a tax reform bill that included tax cuts and a comprehensive overhaul of corporate and individual tax codes, fueling market expectations that the US's robust economic recovery would receive additional cyclical stimulus in the near term. Despite the upturn in activity, core inflation in major advanced economies has remained moderate, further reinforcing market expectations that global interest rates will stay low for an extended period. Against this backdrop, global asset markets surged significantly in 2017, with the U.S. equity market reaching new highs on multiple occasions. However, following the release of stronger-than-expected January wage growth data in the United States, global equity markets reassessed inflation risks. Following short-term volatility in financial markets, the risk of tighter global monetary conditions may continue to cast a shadow over the global economic outlook. In the United States, the economy has already reached its output potential; therefore, the cyclical stimulus from anticipated tax cuts could accelerate a rebound in inflation, prompting the Federal Reserve to tighten monetary policy more rapidly. At the same time, tax cuts may lead to a rise in fiscal deficits, prompting the United States to issue more government bonds in the future. This is expected to exert additional upward pressure on long-term bond yields as the Federal Reserve continues to normalize its balance sheet. Outside the United States, growth momentum in other major advanced economies is strengthening, leading markets to anticipate that their central banks may reduce the scale of their quantitative easing programs. If implemented, this move would lead to a synchronized tightening of global monetary conditions. Policy and event risks arising from international political and geopolitical tensions may also cast a shadow over the global economic growth outlook. The US government appears increasingly inclined to adopt trade protectionist measures to shield domestic industries from competition, with recent examples including the announcement of import tariffs on solar panels, washing machines, steel, and aluminum. These actions raise concerns that trading partners may respond with retaliatory measures. Furthermore, an unexpected escalation in geopolitical tensions could disrupt global trade and heighten volatility in global financial markets. Given the aforementioned uncertainties in the global economic outlook, it remains questionable whether the currently elevated valuations in global asset markets can be sustained. From a fundamental perspective, it remains to be seen whether cyclical global demand growth and expectations of US tax cuts, which are driving higher fiscal deficits, will push up the natural rate of interest (R*). Furthermore, the Federal Reserve's balance sheet normalization is expected to raise term premiums, potentially lifting long-term rates and thereby weighing on asset market valuations. In East Asia, economies within the region are also benefiting from a favorable environment characterized by robust growth and moderate inflation. With solid economic performance and optimistic outlooks, capital has accelerated its inflow, propelling financial markets higher. However, the aforementioned positive outlook faces downside risks from several factors: the synchronized normalization of monetary policies by major central banks, which has tightened global liquidity; the US government's adoption of inward-looking trade policies; escalating geopolitical tensions; and the substantial repatriation of profits by US corporations in response to the one-time "deemed repatriation" provision under the US tax reform. These dynamics may lead to a shortage of offshore US dollar liquidity. Any shocks to credit and financial markets could trigger capital flow reversals, with highly leveraged sectors and economies being the most vulnerable to tightening financial conditions. In Mainland China, the economy performed well in the second half of 2017, supported by steady consumer spending, robust infrastructure investment, and a rebound in industrial spending toward the end of the year. At the same time, signs of the emergence of the "new economy" have become increasingly evident, with high value-added manufacturing and services sectors demonstrating strong business expansion momentum over the past several quarters. Looking ahead, the near-term economic growth outlook remains positive, although uncertainties persist. In particular, to what extent the rapid growth of the "new economy" can offset the short-term pressures on growth posed by further structural reforms remains to be seen. Mainland authorities announced in 2018 that they would continue to pursue an expansionary fiscal policy stance, which could help mitigate adverse economic developments when necessary. During the review period, progress was made in structural reforms and the management of systemic risks. In particular, with the implementation of tightening measures, the Mainland property market showed signs of cooling during the review period, with the most pronounced effects observed in first-tier cities. At the same time, as banks have tightened their lending approval standards, their exposure to enterprises in industries with overcapacity remains under control, while shadow banking activities have also slowed amid financial deleveraging. In addition to the positive developments, our analysis also indicates that the efficiency of capital allocation in Mainland China appears to have improved. In particular, borrowing constraints facing state-owned enterprises (SOEs) with weaker repayment capacities appear to have tightened, likely due to a reduction in support from local governments (see Special Topic 2 on page 28). On the external front, amid a stabilizing economic environment and reduced risks, pressure from capital outflows remained moderate for most of 2017. The Hong Kong economy maintained its quarter-on-quarter growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Real GDP grew by 3.8% for 2017 as a whole, marking the fastest expansion in nearly six years. Private consumption continued to grow steadily in the second half of 2017, supported by robust employment and income conditions and rising asset prices. Overall investment expenditure also rebounded due to an increase in corporate capital expenditure. On the external front, Hong Kong's export performance has improved further, benefiting from the upturn in global trade growth and the gradual recovery of inbound tourism. Nevertheless, because the growth rate of imports outpaced that of exports, net exports of goods continued to drag on GDP growth, while net exports of services made a positive contribution to GDP growth. Economic growth is expected to remain robust in 2018. Domestically, private consumption, building and construction activities, and exports will continue to underpin economic growth. Given that Hong Kong dollar interest rates are expected to rise further, Topic 3 examines the impact of higher mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption. The Government and the market consensus forecast real GDP growth for 2018 to be in the range of 3% to 4% and 3.0%, respectively. However, Hong Kong's growth outlook remains subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including China's economic performance under tighter financial conditions in the external environment mentioned above, as well as trends in Hong Kong's asset markets. Although the unemployment rate fell to a near-20-year low of 2.9%, local inflationary pressures remained under control. However, there have been signs of a slight uptick in monthly inflation dynamics in recent months. Among these, both prices of tradable goods and services rose. Looking ahead, underlying inflation may rise slightly but remain at a moderate level, partly reflecting the pass-through effect of increases in rents for newly leased private residential properties. Tightening liquidity conditions, driven by funding demands from initial public offering activities and seasonal factors, led to an increase in the unwinding of short positions in the Hong Kong dollar, prompting the HKD spot exchange rate to strengthen between September and November 2017. With the easing of liquidity conditions and a resumption of active interest rate arbitrage, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened again from December 2017. In early 2018, despite volatility in global financial markets (particularly in equity markets), the Hong Kong dollar remained broadly stable. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened further in early March 2018, but the currency board guarantee was not triggered. Hong Kong dollar interbank rates faced upward pressure from September to December 2017. This is primarily due to the funding needs from new share issuance activities and banks' prudent approach to liquidity management as the year-end approaches. In December, the average overnight and three-month HIBORs rose by 14 basis points and 50 basis points, respectively, compared to six months prior, reaching 0.25% and 1.26%. The Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) edged down slightly in early January 2018 and has since remained broadly stable, unaffected by recent adjustments in global financial markets. Despite intense competition in the mortgage loan business, the bank's average lending rate on new mortgages continued to rise in line with the upward trend in short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank rates, reaching 2.16% in December. On the other hand, retail banking funding costs remained generally low despite a brief rise in October due to new share issuance activities, with the blended interest rate closing at 0.38% in December. Looking ahead, as the US monetary policy continues to normalize, Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face heightened upward pressure; should global financial market sentiment shift abruptly, volatility in fund flows could increase. In 2017, total bank loans expanded steadily by 16.1% for the full year. Following a robust 10.2% growth in the first half, the loan growth rate moderated to 5.3% in the second half. Among these, the growth rates of both domestic loans and loans for use outside Hong Kong declined across most industries. Growth in foreign currency loans slowed, partly due to higher funding costs in US dollars. Conversely, with a favorable local economic environment and relatively low funding costs in Hong Kong dollars, HKD loans continued to register rapid growth. Due to the faster growth of Hong Kong dollar loans compared to deposits, the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio rose in the second half of 2017, reaching 82.7% by year-end, the highest level since March 2015. On the other hand, due to relatively modest growth in foreign currency loans, the foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio declined to 63.1% at year-end. The onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates against the US dollar showed signs of stabilisation between September and November 2017. Subsequently, as the US dollar weakened significantly against most major currencies, both onshore and offshore RMB exchange rates against the US dollar strengthened from December onwards. Hong Kong's offshore renminbi liquidity pool (comprising total renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit) experienced a slight decline in the first half of the year, followed by a modest recovery in the second half, broadly reflecting changes in market expectations regarding the renminbi exchange rate. Regarding other offshore renminbi business, although renminbi loans continued to decline, the volume of renminbi trade settlement transactions processed by Hong Kong banks rebounded in the second half of the year. The average daily turnover of the RMB Real-Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system remained at a high level. Looking ahead, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from the advancement of the Belt and Road Initiative and the ongoing internationalization of the renminbi.

The synchronized strengthening of the global economy since the latter half of 2016 shows no signs of abating. Improved growth prospects propelled the global equity market to sustain its upward trend in 2017 and early 2018. However, as markets reassessed US inflation risks, global equities faced a wave of selling and significant volatility in February, marking the end of the calm that had prevailed in financial markets over the past two years. Looking ahead, the risks of tightening global financial conditions and a range of policy and event-related risks will continue to cast a shadow over the global outlook. In the context of a tight labor market, US tax cuts could accelerate the cyclical rebound in inflation, prompting the Federal Reserve to tighten monetary policy at a faster pace. As the Federal Reserve continues to normalize its balance sheet, the US Treasury's increased issuance of bonds to fund tax cuts could add upward pressure on long-term bond yields. The shadow of rising trade barriers and the possibility of an unexpected escalation in geopolitical tensions could also threaten the nascent global trade recovery. In East Asia, real economic growth continued to rise in the second half of 2017, supported by robust export performance and stable domestic demand. However, while the economic outlook remains optimistic, it faces several downside risks, including tighter-than-expected global monetary conditions, inward-looking trade policies in the United States, and heightened geopolitical tensions. Should these downside risks materialise, they would also heighten the risk of a reversal in capital flows. Policymakers face multiple challenges: on one hand, they must guard against risks to economic growth, while on the other, they must constrain the impact of prolonged accommodative financial conditions on inflation and balance-sheet vulnerabilities. In Mainland China, economic performance in the second half of 2017 was robust. During the review period, progress was made in structural reforms and in curbing systemic risks. The near-term growth outlook remains positive, although uncertainties persist, partly hinging on the extent to which rapid growth in the "new economy" can offset the short-term pressures on growth arising from further structural reforms. As economic conditions stabilized and risks diminished, capital outflow pressures remained moderate for most of 2017. As the momentum of cyclical economic improvement has solidified since the latter half of 2016, growth in both advanced and emerging market economies accelerated synchronously in 2017. Among the major advanced economies, the United States saw robust growth in both investment and exports, driven by improving private-sector sentiment and a significant depreciation of the US dollar, while the euro area and Japan also recorded broad-based cyclical recoveries. Exports from emerging market economies also benefited from the stabilization of global commodity prices and rising import demand from major advanced economies. In the short term, following the implementation of tax reform in the United States, investment and consumption are expected to receive further stimulus from reductions in corporate and personal income taxes. In light of the current cyclical economic upswing and the expansionary effects of US tax reform, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) forecast in January that global economic growth would accelerate from an estimated 3.7% in 2017 to 3.9% in 2018 (Figure 2.1). Figure 2.1: Forecast for Real GDP Growth. As growth momentum strengthens in the Euro area and Japan, market expectations point to a narrowing divergence in global monetary policy. Coupled with a more optimistic global growth outlook, this is expected to boost risk appetite and trigger capital inflows into emerging market economies, thereby exerting downward pressure on the US dollar. Despite three interest rate hikes by the Federal Reserve during the year and the commencement of balance sheet normalization, the US Dollar Index still declined by nearly 10% in 2017. At the same time, despite broad-based economic acceleration, core inflation in major advanced economies has remained subdued and below central bank targets, leading markets to expect globally low interest rates until recently (Chart 2.2). Against this backdrop, global equity markets continued to rise throughout 2017 and early 2018, with the S&P 500 Index repeatedly setting new highs. This drove the cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio to reach 33.8 in January 2018, its highest level since the dot-com bubble of the early 2000s. Chart 2.2 Core inflation in selected major AEs However, since the second half of 2017, market concerns that tax cuts would widen fiscal deficits and push up inflation have driven a sustained rise in US long-term government bond yields, casting doubt on the sustainability of increasingly elevated asset market valuations. Following the U.S. announcement that average hourly wage growth in January 2018 exceeded expectations, markets reassessed inflation risks in the United States, triggering a correction in global equity markets in early February 2018. The S&P 500 Index fell more than 10% from its high on January 26, wiping out the significant gains posted at the start of the year, and continued to face pressure following the US government's announcement of a new round of trade protection measures in early March. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high in mid-February. Market volatility surged sharply, with the Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index (VIX) spiking to a two-year high of 37.3, marking the end of a prolonged period of subdued volatility over the past two years (Chart 2.3). Chart 2.3 Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index (VIX) Looking ahead, after a period of short-term equity market volatility, risks such as US inflation, upward pressure on US long-term bond yields, and potential monetary policy tightening by other major central banks could lead to tighter global financial conditions, thereby casting a shadow over the global economic outlook. First, regarding US inflation risks, the recently enacted tax reform includes several provisions that are expected to provide short-term cyclical stimulus to private consumption and investment. The key measures involved in the tax reform include: (1) reductions in corporate and individual income tax rates; (2) temporary full expensing of capital investments; and (3) a one-time "deemed repatriation" provision designed to reduce the incentive for U.S. companies to retain earnings offshore. While it remains uncertain how tax cuts will affect domestic demand and inflation, given that the US economy has already reached its potential output, tax cuts could push US output beyond potential levels, thereby leading to an overheating economy and a cyclical rebound in inflation. If inflationary pressures rise more than expected, the Federal Reserve may be prompted to accelerate its monetary tightening. Currently, financial market expectations for the path of the Fed Funds rate are more subdued than the Federal Reserve's own projections. However, should inflation unexpectedly rebound, there is a risk that market expectations for rate hikes could be abruptly revised upward (Chart 2.4). Nevertheless, due to (1) an anticipated increase in fiscal deficits leading to a decline in the national savings rate, and (2) corporate tax cuts and more favorable tax treatment for capital expenditure potentially raising the investment rate, the US R* may face upside risks in the future. With robust local demand and an improvement in export performance, the Hong Kong economy maintained solid growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Economic growth is expected to remain robust in 2018. The Hong Kong economic outlook remains influenced by numerous uncertainties and risks, including the normalization of monetary policy by major central banks, the stability of global financial markets, the rising sentiment of protectionism, and the escalation of geopolitical tensions. In the near term, while local inflation pressures are expected to remain mild, several upside risks persist. The Hong Kong economy maintained its growth momentum in the second half of 2017. On a seasonally adjusted basis, the quarter-on-quarter growth rate of real GDP was 0.8% in both the third and fourth quarters, similar to the average growth rate of 0.9% in the preceding two quarters (Chart 3.1). Compared with the first half of the year, private consumption continued to grow steadily and remained one of the key drivers of local GDP growth. Consumption growth remained robust, supported by favourable employment and income conditions, optimistic consumer sentiment, and the positive impact of rising asset prices through the wealth effect. Although building and construction activities weakened, increased corporate capital expenditure led to a significant rise in overall investment spending in the final quarter, following three quarters of relatively stable performance. On the external front, Hong Kong's export performance is set to further improve, benefiting from the upturn in global trade growth and the gradual recovery of inbound tourism (Chart 3.2). Nevertheless, because the growth rate of imports outpaced that of exports, net exports of goods continued to drag on GDP growth, while net exports of services made a positive contribution to GDP growth. Chart 3.2 Robust growth momentum in real exports and imports sustained employment, leading to an increase in job vacancies in the second half of 2017. During the period, total employment increased by approximately 0.7% to over 3.85 million, with the most significant growth observed in the construction, financial, and commercial and business services sectors, as well as in public administration, social, and personal services. Labour productivity showed further improvement, as real GDP growth outpaced the growth in employment. Economic growth is expected to remain robust in 2018. On the external front, Hong Kong's export performance will continue to benefit from an improving global economic growth outlook and the gradual recovery of inbound tourism. Domestically, private consumption is expected to continue growing, primarily driven by favourable conditions in the labour market. Given that HKD interest rates are expected to rise further, Topic 3 examines the impact of higher mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption. Regarding gross fixed capital formation in the local economy, with an increase in housing supply and the continued rollout of infrastructure projects, building and construction activities are expected to grow steadily. While an improving economic environment is likely to stimulate business capital expenditure, potential interest rate hikes could have a negative impact. The Government forecasts real GDP growth for 2018 in the range of 3% to 4%, while growth estimates from international organizations and private-sector analysts range from 2% to 4%. However, Hong Kong's growth outlook remains subject to numerous risks and uncertainties, including mainland China's economic performance amid tighter financial conditions in the external environment, as discussed in earlier chapters, as well as trends in Hong Kong's asset markets. Local inflationary pressures remained under control in the second half of 2017, although there were signs of a slight uptick in month-on-month inflation momentum in recent months. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying composite consumer price index rose by 1.7% and 1.6% in the third and fourth quarters, respectively, roughly in line with the average increase of about 1.7% in the first half of the year. However, the annualized three-month-on-three-month underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, edged up slightly to 2.8% in January 2018 (Chart 3.3). Among these, both prices of tradable goods and services rose. The recovery in fresh-letting private residential rentals since mid-2016 may have also contributed to upward pressure on inflation to some extent (Chart 3.4). Moreover, labour cost pressures continued to remain moderate in recent quarters (Chart 3.5). On the external front, if global inflation or commodity prices register a surprise increase, it could bolster domestic inflationary pressures. On the domestic front, the labor market has tightened further in recent times, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling from 3.4% in 2016 to 2.9% in December 2017, marking the first time in nearly two decades that it dropped below 3% (Chart 3.6). Following the 2008 global financial crisis, low interest rates led to an increase in household mortgage debt in Hong Kong. As the normalization of US interest rates advances, Hong Kong dollar interest rates are expected to rise in tandem, leading to a corresponding increase in household mortgage repayment burdens and, consequently, dampening household consumption. Accordingly, this专题 study examines the impact of rising mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption in Hong Kong. Mortgage repayment burden refers to the proportion of mortgage debt service payments (i.e., interest payments plus principal repayments) relative to income. Figure B3.1 illustrates the role of mortgage repayment burden in transmitting interest rate shocks to private consumption. In addition to the substitution effect, income effect, wealth effect, and collateral effect associated with asset price changes as discussed in general economic theory, interest rate shocks can also affect private consumption by altering mortgage interest payments, thereby changing household disposable income, particularly under conditions of mortgage repayment burden. This impact will be magnified as the outstanding mortgage loan balance increases. Furthermore, mortgage principal repayments will fluctuate with changes in the outstanding mortgage balance, which in turn affects private consumption by altering household disposable income. Figure B3.1 Determinants of private consumption To measure the impact of mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption, we estimated the Outstanding Mortgage Debt Service Ratio (OMDSR) based on outstanding mortgage liabilities. In contrast to the existing mortgage burden indicator, which applies only to new mortgage liabilities, the OMDSR covers all outstanding mortgage liabilities across households, which are more closely linked to total private consumption. We broadly adopt the methodology used by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) to measure the overall mortgage debt servicing ratio (OMDSR) using the standard formula for fixed-installment mortgages: where Dt represents the outstanding amount of residential mortgage loans in the banking sector, Yt denotes the total income of owner-occupier households (measured as the median income of owner-occupier households multiplied by the number of owner-occupier households), and rt and st represent the average interest rate and average loan term of the outstanding mortgage loans, respectively. To assess whether the OMDSR can reliably measure mortgage payment burdens across the entire household sector, it is advisable to compare the OMDSR with two commonly used debt service burden indicators. Figure B3.2 shows the estimates of the overall mortgage debt service ratio (OMDSR) from 1985 to 2017, alongside the median mortgage repayment-to-income and loan repayment-to-income ratios estimated by the Census and Statistics Department based on quinquennial population censuses. In the early 2000s, both ratios exhibited a downward trend, consistent with the decline in overall household mortgage lending and a sharp fall in mortgage interest rates following the bursting of the property market bubble in 1997. Despite the sharp rise in property prices following the global financial crisis, both ratios remained stable, owing to the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's macro-prudential measures on bank mortgage lending, which curbed overall household mortgage leverage. Furthermore, the extension of loan terms for new mortgage loans has also reduced the actual amount of mortgage repayments. Figure B3.2: OMDSR and the median debt-service-to-income ratio for mortgage repayments and loan repayments. We also compare the OMDSR with banks' debt-service-to-income ratio, which reflects the actual debt-service-to-income ratio of new mortgage applicants at the banks. As shown in Figure B3.3, the OMDSR is lower than banks' DSRs, partly because the OMDSR covers both new and existing mortgages. Since the original mortgages were originated when property prices were lower, their monthly repayments are correspondingly lower than those of newly originated mortgages. Therefore, the outstanding mortgage debt servicing ratio (OMDSR), which covers both existing and newly approved mortgages, will be lower than the debt servicing ratio for newly approved mortgages alone (i.e., the banks' debt servicing ratio). Furthermore, the relatively high debt-service-to-income ratio of banks also stems from their compliance with the HKMA's prudential regulatory requirements, which mandate that non-mortgage loan repayments be factored into the calculation of the debt-service-to-income ratio. Following the global financial crisis, both the overall mortgage debt service ratio (OMDSR) and banks' debt service-to-income (DSR) ratios have remained stable, largely due to the HKMA's implementation of prudential mortgage lending regulations that set ceilings on banks' DSRs. This measure has also helped to dampen fluctuations in the OMDSR. As shown in Figure B3.3, the OMDSR and banks' new mortgage DSRs have generally aligned with conventional mortgage burden indicators. However, the OMDSR offers greater timeliness and captures the burden of total outstanding mortgage liabilities, not merely that of newly originated mortgages. Therefore, we believe that the OMDSR can be used to assess the impact of mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption. To assess the impact of mortgage repayment burden on private consumption in Hong Kong, we estimate an error-correction model following the approaches of Lai and Lam (2002) and Kang (2016). Among these, the long-term relationship between real private consumption (measured by real private consumption per household) and its determinants is represented in the short-term equation by an error-correction term. Based on existing theories and empirical evidence, we identify real income (measured by the median household income deflated by the Composite Consumer Price Index), real housing and financial wealth (proxied by residential property prices and the Hang Seng Index, respectively, also deflated by the Composite Consumer Price Index), and the OMDSR as long-term determinants of private consumption.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened, while the local interbank market continued to operate in an orderly manner. In the second half of 2017, total loans continued to increase, albeit at a slower pace compared to the first half. Looking ahead, as the US monetary policy continues to normalize, the Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face greater upward pressure. If global financial market sentiment shifts sharply, capital flow volatility could increase. In the second half of 2017, the spot exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar against the US dollar fluctuated between 7.799 and 7.827 (Chart 4.1). The Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate briefly strengthened between September and November 2017 and remained at a level around 7.80. This was primarily due to increased funding requirements from new share issuance activities and banks' prudent approach to liquidity management at month-end and year-end, which tightened liquidity conditions, slowed down interest rate arbitrage activities, and led to an increase in covering of short Hong Kong dollar positions. As Hong Kong dollar liquidity constraints eased and year-end demand for US dollars in commercial transactions rose, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate softened again in mid-December 2017. Entering 2018, despite increased volatility in global financial markets (particularly equity markets), the Hong Kong dollar continued to operate in an orderly manner. During the reporting period, the Hong Kong dollar depreciated against the US dollar, but the currency board peg was not triggered (Chart 4.2). Despite the Federal Reserve's rate hikes and ongoing balance sheet reductions, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2017 and in recent periods. The liquidity positions of the banking sector remained sound during the review period, as measured by the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) requirements under Basel III. Meanwhile, the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (LMR) of category 2 institutions declined slightly from 49.7% in the second quarter of 2017 to 49.4% in the fourth quarter, yet it remained well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. The ample liquidity of Authorised Institutions indicates that the Hong Kong banking sector is well positioned to withstand liquidity shocks that could arise from potential outflows of funds from Hong Kong.
