Drawing on the experience of the 2003 SARS outbreak, these effects may be short-lived; however, the actual outcome will depend on the severity and geographic spread of the pandemic, as well as the effectiveness of government measures to contain its outbreak. At the same time, East Asian economies are also facing multiple headwinds. First, although market expectations point to a short-term deterioration in corporate earnings (Chart 2.8), the globally accommodative monetary stance has encouraged yield-seeking activities, thereby pushing up asset prices without fundamental support. Therefore, regional stock markets are more susceptible to shifts in investor sentiment. Figure 2.8 Expected returns of constituent stocks of the benchmark equity index. Second, weaker corporate earnings and economic growth may make it more difficult for private sector entities in the region to service their debt. While a decline in local interest rates may provide breathing room for indebted companies and households, it could also sow the seeds for further debt accumulation. Furthermore, as noted in Topic 1, increased inflows of index-tracking funds into regional financial markets could exacerbate the risk of private sector debt overhang, although this impact may be limited to financially sounder firms and their long-term borrowing. Third, regarding external factors, the risks facing East Asian economies may increase in the face of increasingly protectionist US trade policies. Despite recent progress in the Phase One China-US trade agreement, trade tensions between the two countries persist due to the continued existence of fundamental trade issues. As shown in Figure 2.9, the persistent rise in trade surpluses between the United States and several economies within the region suggests that multinational corporations may continue to seek additional supply channels beyond China-centric supply chains to circumvent tariffs. As of November 2019, the cumulative trade surplus with the United States of nine emerging Asian economies (excluding China) had risen to approximately $167 billion. If trade surpluses with the United States continue to widen, certain Asian economies could become the next targets in the trade war; for instance, the US government imposed steep tariffs of up to 456% on steel imports from Vietnam in July 2019. 7. In light of this, despite the truce between China and the United States, the outlook for intra-regional trade remains highly uncertain. Figure 2.9: Surplus in US goods trade Over the past decade, the deepening integration of global financial markets has led to a significant increase in cross-border securities investment capital flows worldwide. A recent study indicates that as much as 70% of these cross-border investment fund flows are driven by index-tracking funds. 8. Index-driven funds encompass not only funds that closely track investment indices (commonly referred to as passive funds) but also actively managed funds that reference investment indices. 9. By introducing overseas investors that would otherwise be unable to attract or access these emerging market economies, these funds help advance the development of their financial markets. Therefore, such funds contribute to diversifying the investor base for emerging market economies, supporting long-term growth and stability in these markets. However, is there really such a thing as a free lunch? In the case of passive bond funds, market concerns persist that such investments could undermine the fiscal discipline of corporate bond issuers, potentially leading to elevated leverage levels for these companies. 10. Moreover, some argue that the recent growth of index-tracking funds has exacerbated volatility in global securities investment capital flows, rendering emerging market economies—which are already highly sensitive to global factors and influenced by common drivers—more vulnerable. 11 This topic assesses the impact of index-driven investment on financial stability with respect to these two propositions. Passive bond funds allocate their investment capital to relevant bonds in accordance with the weightings of constituent bonds within the benchmark index. Therefore, compared with actively managed bond funds, the mechanized investment decisions adopted by passive bond funds may reduce the incentive for issuers of index constituent bonds to act in the interests of fund investors. 13 Moreover, from a financial stability perspective, such behavior could foster excessive borrowing, posing significant credit and debt-servicing risks to corporate sectors in emerging market economies that have seen leverage ratios surge sharply since the global financial crisis (Figure B1.1). Figure B1.1 Corporate leverage in emerging market economies: We estimate the weight of each emerging market economy's corporate bond issuers in a leading index tracking emerging market corporate bonds as a proxy for their exposure to passive bond fund investment.¹⁴ We find that such investment increases the long-term (rather than short-term) leverage ratios of the relevant corporate issuers. The blue solid bars in Chart B1.2 represent the estimated effects. In addition to promoting the development of the corporate bond market in emerging market economies, the expansion of the long-term investor base driven by passive bond funds also benefits corporate development in these economies. We also find that the aforementioned effect is statistically significant only for firms from emerging market economies with robust fundamentals (particularly stronger solvency and lower leverage ratios), as illustrated by the solid green bars in Chart B1.2. Facing higher costs of financial distress, highly leveraged firms or those with weaker debt-servicing capacity appear less likely to fall further into a debt trap due to passive bond fund investment. In summary, the above findings suggest that the growth in passive bond fund investment may not significantly increase the debt-servicing risk for the corporate sector of emerging market economies.

Due to weakened private consumption, reduced investment expenditure, and underperforming exports, Hong Kong's economy contracted in the second half of 2019, marking its first recession since 2009. The economic performance in 2020 is expected to face significant challenges, and the recent outbreak of the coronavirus has introduced substantial downside risks. The economic outlook is subject to a range of uncertainties and risks, including slowing global economic growth, China-US trade relations, mainland China's economic performance, and the evolution of local social developments. Given various headwinds facing the economy, the unemployment rate may rise further in 2020. Local inflation pressures are expected to ease, though the outlook faces potential upside and downside risks. Hong Kong's economy contracted significantly in the second half of 2019. Year on year, real GDP contracted by 2.8% and 2.9% in the third and fourth quarters, respectively (Table 3.A). Dragged down by economic contraction in the second half of the year, the full-year economy shrank by 1.2%, a marked deterioration from the 2.9% growth recorded in 2018 and marking the first annual contraction since the global financial crisis of 2009. Chart 3.1 Quarter-on-quarter real GDP growth and contribution by major expenditure components: Economic activity slowed significantly in the second half of the year (Chart 3.1). Specifically, real GDP fell sequentially by 0.4% in the second quarter, 3.0% in the third quarter, and 0.3% in the fourth quarter, indicating that the economy had entered a recession. Domestically, private consumption was the main factor dragging down the third-quarter GDP. Local social events severely impacted consumption activities, weakening the economic outlook and eroding consumer confidence, leading to a significant contraction in private consumption from the third quarter onwards. 33. Amid rising economic uncertainties and a deterioration in business sentiment, total investment spending remained weak, weighing on fourth-quarter GDP. Externally, amid escalating US-China trade tensions, weakening global economic growth, and a sharp decline in visitor arrivals to Hong Kong, Hong Kong's foreign trade performance remained subdued (Chart 3.2). 35 Under the sharp contraction in services exports, net trade weighed on GDP in the third quarter but provided support to GDP growth in the fourth quarter, partly reflecting an improvement in the goods trade balance. Figure 3.2: Real Imports and Exports In view of the significant headwinds facing the economy, the government introduced a series of measures between August and December 2019 to alleviate the financial burden on residents, safeguard employment, and support businesses, with particular emphasis on small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and sectors severely impacted, such as retail, food and beverage services, transportation, and tourism. 36. To provide banks with greater capacity to intensify support for the local economy and help mitigate economic cycles, the HKMA announced on 14 October that the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for banks would be reduced from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby enabling banks to release an additional HK$200 billion to HK$300 billion in lending capacity for enterprises, including small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Hong Kong's economic performance in 2020 is expected to face significant challenges, and the recent pandemic has introduced notable downside risks. Since some sectors have yet to recover from the disruption caused by the social unrest, the pandemic will deliver a double blow to these industries. However, the countercyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 Budget provided assistance to households and businesses (particularly small and medium-sized enterprises), including one-off cash handouts to adult permanent residents and special low-interest loans with 100% government guarantees for enterprises under the Small and Medium Enterprise Financing Guarantee Scheme. On March 16, 2020, the HKMA further reduced the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for banks from 2.0% to 1.0%, thereby providing banks with greater capacity to strengthen support for the local economy, particularly for sectors and individuals facing heightened pressure in the short term due to the pandemic. By component of GDP, given the fragility of consumption and business confidence, private consumption and investment are likely to remain weak. While government consumption is expected to support economic growth, public investment spending is likely to remain subdued as some major infrastructure projects near completion. On the external front, the Phase One US-China trade agreement is expected to have a modest positive impact on the local economy in the short term. 38. However, the sluggish global economic growth and trade activity will continue to weigh on Hong Kong's foreign trade performance. In particular, the outbreak of coronavirus could lead to disruptions in regional supply chains and a slowdown in cross-border economic activities (such as tourism), thereby constraining Hong Kong's export performance. The Government forecasts real GDP growth for 2020 in the range of -1.5% to 0.5%, while the average growth forecast by international organizations and private-sector analysts stands at -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is subject to a number of uncertainties and risks as discussed in previous chapters. The labour market faced heightened pressure in the second half of 2019 and the early months of 2020. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.3% in December 2019, and further climbed to 3.7% in February 2020 (Chart 3.3). Among these, unemployment rates in the retail, accommodation, and food services sectors rose further to a near-decade high of 6.1%, partly reflecting the severe impact of social unrest. 39 As economic momentum waned, total employment fell by 0.5% year-on-year in the second half of 2019 and continued to decline to 3,768,800 in February 2020. Among these, the decline in employment was mainly in the trade, wholesale and retail, accommodation, food services, and construction sectors. Real wages also declined by 0.3% year-on-year in the third quarter. Looking ahead, given the aforementioned weak economic outlook, the labour market will continue to face greater challenges, with the unemployment rate likely to rise further. Topic 3 will provide a more detailed examination of recent developments and the short-term outlook for the labour market. Chart 3.3 Labour market conditions. Local inflationary pressures continued to build up until the third quarter of 2019, primarily driven by rising fresh pork prices; subsequently, as economic activity weakened, inflationary momentum gradually moderated. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying composite consumer price index rose by 3.3% in the third quarter, with the pace of increase moderating slightly to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. The underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum and is calculated as the annualised three-month-on-three-month rate, also eased from a high of 4.7% in August 2019 to 2.1% in January 2020. The moderation in inflationary momentum was driven by reduced price pressures across several components of consumer price indices. In the case of traded goods, rising fresh pork prices kept basic food inflation notably elevated, while price pressures on consumer goods such as clothing and durable goods remained moderate. In the services sector, with the recent slowdown in rent increases for newly leased private residential properties, the growth of the rental component in the Consumer Price Index also trended downward (Chart 3.5). Labour cost pressures rose slightly but remained moderate in recent quarters (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.4 Different measures of consumer price inflation Chart 3.5 Rental component of the composite consumer price index and market rentals Chart 3.6 Unit labour costs Local inflationary pressures are expected to ease in the near term. Locally, the weak economic conditions and a widening negative output gap will continue to exert downward pressure on inflation. With private residential rentals continuing to moderate, the housing rental component in inflation is expected to ease further. On the external front, with weak global economic growth and soft energy prices, imported inflation is expected to remain moderate. Market consensus forecasts headline inflation for 2020 to range between 0.6% and 3.7%, while the Government projects underlying inflation at 2.5% and headline inflation at 1.7%. This inflation outlook is subject to both upside and downside risk factors. On the one hand, given that the estimated negative output gap has widened since the third quarter of 2019, a more severe deterioration in the economy than expected (for instance, due to the prolonged impact of the coronavirus pandemic) could further dampen inflation. On the other hand, if the disruption to fresh pork supplies becomes more severe, it could exert upward pressure on inflation. Despite the clear slowdown in Hong Kong's economy, the unemployment rate remained at a low level of 2.8–2.9% during the first nine months of 2019. As social events persisted, the unemployment rate rose more noticeably to 3.3% by the end of 2019. The labor market is expected to face greater headwinds in 2020 due to the impact of the coronavirus pandemic. Against this backdrop, this专题 examines recent developments and near-term prospects in the labour market, including an analysis of why the overall labour market remained broadly resilient in the first three quarters of 2019 (with the unemployment rate showing little change) and what this implies for future developments. This report also examines risk factors that could lead to a sharp rise in the unemployment rate. It is worth noting that, in part due to the costs associated with adjusting labor demand, the unemployment rate is a lagging indicator. In fact, the unemployment rate typically lags behind the year-on-year growth rate of real GDP by about two to three quarters (Chart B3.1). This lagging nature helps explain why, when real economic activity deteriorated sharply in the third quarter, the unemployment rate remained low at around 2.9%. Chart B3.1 Real GDP Growth Rate and Unemployment Rate In terms of labour demand, while the escalating trade tensions between China and the United States and local social unrest respectively dealt heavy blows to employment in trade-related, retail, and tourism sectors, several key industries continued to underpin the overall labour market. Specifically, employment in the financial, business, public administration, social and personal services sectors continued to grow in 2019, partly offsetting the decline in employment in the trade and retail sectors (Figure B3.2). Despite the economy entering a recession, Hong Kong's financial system remained resilient, and financial activity in fintech development and new share issuances was particularly robust. These factors are likely to support the employment market in the financial and business services sector. Furthermore, the public administration, social and personal services sectors, including education, healthcare, and social work, appear to be less sensitive to economic cycles. Correlation analysis indicates that while employment in many sectors is highly correlated with real GDP, the public administration, social, and personal services sector exhibits a more neutral response to economic cycles. In other words, even if the economy slows, employment in these sectors may not be significantly affected by cyclical fluctuations. Figure B3.2 Change in employment by industry in 2019  On the supply side, the labour force participation rate, which was 40, declined from 61.2% in 2018 to 60.5% in 2019, providing a buffer for the rise in the unemployment rate. Figure B3.3 shows the supply and demand factors that influenced changes in the unemployment rate (blue line). As shown in the chart, the labor force participation rate (green bars) exerted downward pressure on the unemployment rate in 2019. On the other hand, the increase in employment in the first half of 2019 (shown by the purple bars) also helped to suppress the unemployment rate. However, the economy contracted significantly in the second half of the year, with a decline in employment placing upward pressure on the unemployment rate. Overall, although employment declined during the economic downturn, the lower labor force participation rate helped mitigate upward pressure on the unemployment rate in the second half of 2019. Figure B3.3 Factors Contributing to Changes in the Unemployment Rate. Some structural shifts in the labour market are also worth noting. In particular, the increasing proportion of voluntary part-time employees may help companies retain their staff. In fact, the proportion of self-employed and underemployed individuals in total employment has declined in recent years to 6% and 1%, respectively, while the number of voluntary part-time workers has continued to rise, making them the second-largest group among the total employed population (approximately 7% in 2017). 42. Accordingly, companies could retain or recruit more staff by adjusting the working hours of part-time employees. Our calculations indicate that average weekly working hours have declined, falling from a recent high of 48 hours in April 2010 to approximately 44 hours at present, partly reflecting a higher proportion of part-time workers in the current workforce.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has strengthened since October, with upward momentum intensifying in December, resulting in the currency remaining within the strong-side conversion range over recent months. The robust demand for the Hong Kong dollar stemmed partly from equity-related factors and partly from the unwinding of short positions in the Hong Kong dollar as liquidity tightened toward year-end. Overall, Hong Kong's foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate smoothly and in an orderly manner. Despite the uncertain external environment and the possibility that the coronavirus outbreak could heighten market sentiment and exacerbate capital flow volatility, Hong Kong possesses ample foreign reserves and a robust banking system, enabling it to withstand pressures from capital outflows without compromising the territory's financial stability. Supported by increased demand for Hong Kong dollars related to equities (including initial public offerings), the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has gradually strengthened since mid-October (Figure 4.1). Entering December, the upward momentum of the Hong Kong dollar intensified further. From mid-December through February, the exchange rate remained within the strong-side conversion range. The Hong Kong dollar strengthened, partly due to robust initial public offering (IPO) activities and partly because tighter liquidity near year-end prompted the unwinding of short positions in the Hong Kong dollar. Following the Lunar New Year holiday, liquidity conditions eased, leading to a slight softening of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate, which closed at 7.7956 on February 28. Overall, during the review period, HKD trading remained smooth and orderly. As the strong and weak Convertibility Undertakings were not triggered during the review period, the Aggregate Balance remained unchanged at around HK$54.0 billion (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Hong Kong Dollar Exchange Rate  Chart 4.2 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes (EFBNs)  The Hong Kong dollar's nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER) broadly tracked movements in the US dollar and registered a slight increase during the review period (Chart 4.3). Given the small inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, which had a limited impact on the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate (REER) index, the REER index generally followed the trend of the nominal effective exchange rate (NEER) index. Chart 4.3 Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rates In measuring capital flows in Hong Kong, it is essential to distinguish between two distinct yet interrelated concepts of capital flows: (1) HKD-denominated capital flows; and (2) cross-border capital flows. The focus of the Hong Kong dollar fund flow analysis lies in the monetary dimension of capital flows, which aids in assessing monetary stability, particularly under the Linked Exchange Rate System. On the other hand, cross-border capital flows, which focus on the movement of funds through Hong Kong's banking system across regions, contribute to assessing the overall stability of Hong Kong's financial system. Two capital flow concepts require distinct monitoring indicators. When monitoring HKD capital flows, attention should be paid to the HKD exchange rate and the surplus/deficit balance. If the public or investors were to significantly convert their HKD-denominated assets into foreign currency assets, demand for the HKD would naturally decline, leading to a depreciation of the HKD exchange rate. Under the Linked Exchange Rate System, if the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakens to the weak-side conversion rate of HKD 7.85 per USD, the Monetary Authority stands ready to purchase Hong Kong dollars at banks' request upon demand, thereby reducing the monetary base. Since April 2019, the aggregate balance has remained broadly unchanged, and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has been trading near the strong-side conversion rate in recent months; accordingly, no significant capital outflow from the Hong Kong dollar was observed during the review period. In monitoring cross-border capital flows, the total amount of bank deposits in Hong Kong serves as a useful indicator. When there is substantial outflow of funds from the Hong Kong banking system, bank deposits necessarily decline. During the review period, total deposits grew at a moderate pace, indicating no significant cross-border capital outflow. The Hong Kong foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate in a smooth and orderly manner, indicating that the impact of the coronavirus pandemic on the local monetary environment remains limited. However, we need to closely monitor the risks arising from the outbreak of the coronavirus pandemic. Hong Kong possesses substantial foreign exchange reserves and a resilient banking sector, and the Monetary Authority has the capacity, resources, and determination to address capital outflows and maintain Hong Kong's monetary and financial stability. Despite an uncertain external environment and a slowdown in the local economy, Hong Kong's monetary conditions remained relatively accommodative during the review period. The HKD monetary base remained sizeable, rising by 4.0% from end-June 2020 to HK$1,689.4 billion at the end of January 2021 (Chart 4.4). As the Convertibility Undertakings were not triggered during this period, the aggregate balance remained largely unchanged at approximately HK$54 billion. Other components of the monetary base, including outstanding Exchange Fund bills and bonds, deposit-taking certificates, and government-issued circulating notes and coins, continued to rise steadily. Chart 4.4 Composition of the Monetary Base During the review period, broad HK dollar monetary supply indicators remained broadly stable. Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (HKD M3) increased by 3.5% in the first half of 2019 and subsequently rose marginally by 0.2% over the seven-month period since end-June 2019. Analysis of corresponding assets shows that the growth in M3 in Hong Kong dollars since end-June 2022 was mainly driven by an increase in banks' net foreign currency assets and a rise in the monetary base (due to higher outstanding liabilities certificates and government-issued circulating notes and coins) (Chart 4.5). Over the seven-month period since the end of June, Hong Kong dollar deposits, a major component of Hong Kong dollar M3, remained broadly unchanged (Chart 4.6). In Hong Kong dollar deposits, time deposits continued to grow moderately, partly reflecting the rise in Hong Kong dollar deposit rates. Chart 4.5 Changes in Hong Kong Dollar M3 and Corresponding Assets. In the seven-month period since end-June 2019, foreign currency deposits increased modestly by 2.3% (Chart 4.6), driven primarily by US dollar deposits, which rose by 3.5% over the same period. Other foreign currency deposits fell by 1.0% during the same period, with RMB-denominated deposits (converted into Hong Kong dollars) recording a slight decline. Overall, total deposits with authorized institutions increased steadily by 1.2% since end-June. Supported by the increase in total deposits, the broad money supply in Hong Kong also rose at a relatively stable pace. The total money supply measures M2 and M3 increased by 1.6% and 1.5%, respectively, since the end of June (Chart 4.7). Given that monthly monetary statistics may be subject to volatility due to various short-term factors, such as seasonal fluctuations, funding demands related to initial public offerings (IPOs), and business and investment-related activities, these figures should be interpreted with caution. Chart 4.6 Deposits of authorized institutions by currency Chart 4.7 Aggregate M2 money supply Although the monetary environment remained relatively accommodative, short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates exhibited volatility, reflecting seasonal liquidity demands and increased capital market activity since the fourth quarter of 2019. In particular, the Hong Kong stock market experienced heightened initial public offering activity, leading to pronounced fluctuations in the Hong Kong dollar interbank overnight rate in late October and mid-November (Chart 4.8). 44 During the review period, other short-term Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) generally rose. Significant upward pressure on overnight interbank rates is exerted by large-scale new share listings. This situation may arise when market participants anticipate the future subscription deadline for major new share listings in advance and thereby prepare interim funding to deploy capital ahead of schedule. Compared to the end of June 2019, the yield on 10-year Hong Kong Government bonds fell by 60 basis points to 1.04% on February 28, 2020 (Chart 4.9). At the same time, the yield on 3-year Hong Kong government bonds fell by 50 basis points over the same period to 1.00%. Chart 4.9 Government Bond Yields, Composite Interest Rates, and Average Interest Rates on New Mortgage Loans On the retail front, the composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, gradually increased from 0.94% at the end of July 2019 to 1.01% at the end of January 2020. This rise mainly reflects the bank's continued adjustment of preferential deposit rates upward to attract deposit funds, thereby raising the weighted average deposit rate in Hong Kong dollars. In late October 2019, following the reduction in the target range for the US federal funds rate, several retail banks lowered their Best Lending Rates by 12.5 basis points. Therefore, the Best Lending Rate in retail banking currently ranges from 5.00% to 5.50%. In terms of mortgage loans, for those benchmarked on the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR), major banks raised the interest rate cap calculated based on their Best Lending Rates, causing the average interest rate on new mortgage loans in October to rise to around 2.63%. 45 The Best Lending Rate in the market has declined since November, leading to a slight decrease in the average mortgage rate to 2.53% in January 2020. Amid evolving risks posed by the coronavirus pandemic to US economic activity and in support of the Federal Reserve's policy objectives, the Fed lowered the target range for the federal funds rate by a total of 150 basis points to 0–0.25% on March 3 (US time) and March 15 (US time). While Hong Kong interbank offered rates (HIBORs) have, in the long term, followed movements in US dollar interest rates, short-term HIBORs may be influenced by local factors affecting demand for Hong Kong dollars, such as new share listings in the territory. The banking system's net surplus has declined since April 2018, potentially increasing the sensitivity of HIBORs to changes in the supply and demand for Hong Kong dollar funding. However, this does not imply that the current Aggregate Balance of HK$54 billion is insufficient to meet the interbank payment and settlement needs of the banking system. In fact, Hong Kong's interbank market has continued to operate in an orderly manner. In the event of short-term liquidity tightening, banks may utilize the liquidity facilities provided by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority. Given the potential escalation of US-China trade tensions, the offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates weakened significantly in late August and September 2019. The offshore renminbi fell to a ten-year low of 7.19 against the US dollar on September 2 (Chart 4.10). Entering October, market optimism about the resumption of trade negotiations between China and the United States led to a reversal of the renminbi's depreciation trend. Both the offshore and onshore renminbi strengthened in the fourth quarter and, following the signing of the US-China Phase One trade deal, briefly surpassed the 6.9 level in mid-January 2020. However, since late January, the outbreak of the coronavirus has once again placed downward pressure on both offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates. From May to August, the offshore renminbi (CNH) traded at a discount to the onshore renminbi (CNY) for most of the period, while from late 2019 onwards it generally traded at a premium. In late January 2020, the discount briefly widened, though the spread remained moderate by historical standards. Figure 4.10 Onshore and Offshore RMB Exchange Rates Despite volatility in the RMB exchange rate, liquidity conditions in the CNH interbank market remained broadly stable during the review period. During the review period, the three-month offshore renminbi (CNH) Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) continued to hover in the 3% to 4% range (Chart 4.11). The overnight offshore RMB Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate experienced brief fluctuations in late August and late November 2020 due to MSCI's A-share index rebalancing by Morgan Stanley International Capital, and again at the end of January 2020 as the Lunar New Year holiday approached.

Due to increased uncertainties in the global and local economic environment, profitability of Hong Kong's retail banks declined slightly in the second half of 2019. Nevertheless, the capitalisation and liquidity positions of the Hong Kong banking sector remain strong and sound by international standards. By historical standards, asset quality remains at a healthy level. Although the growth rate of total loans slowed in the second half of the previous year, it still outpaced the growth of total deposits during the review period. Accordingly, the average loan-to-deposit ratio in all currencies and the loan-to-deposit ratio in Hong Kong dollars for all authorized institutions both increased. However, given that the aggregate balances in the banking system remained at stable levels and deposits were broadly steady, liquidity conditions in the banking sector remained sound. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will continue to face multiple downside risks stemming from uncertainties related to the spread of coronavirus, future US-China trade relations, escalating geopolitical tensions, and local social developments. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage levels and household debt burdens, banks should prudently assess the potential impact of these risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. In the second half of 2019, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks, at HK$59 billion, decreased slightly by 1.5% compared with the same period in 2018. Accordingly, the return on assets declined marginally to 1.13% in the second half of 2019, down from 1.23% in the same period of 2018 (Chart 5.1). Although the net interest margin (NIM) of retail banks narrowed slightly from 1.67% in the second half of 2018 to 1.63% in the same period of 2019 (Chart 5.2), net interest income of retail banks continued to grow moderately throughout the review period. However, loan impairment provisions and operating expenses in retail banking both increased, resulting in a slight decline in profits. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Despite the US Federal Funds target rate being cut three times by 25 basis points each in the second half of 2019, the HKD wholesale funding market has not yet experienced significant downward pressure. In contrast, driven by several local factors—including seasonal funding demand, heightened liquidity requirements associated with major initial public offerings, and tighter interbank market liquidity conditions—the short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates have exhibited an upward trend since the fourth quarter of 2019. At the same time, during the review period, HKD interbank interest rates for longer maturities remained broadly stable. The three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) stood at 2.43% by the end of 2019, close to the level six months earlier (blue line in Chart 5.3). On the retail front, given that Hong Kong dollar (HKD) savings deposit rates remain close to zero, local banks have limited scope to follow the US Federal Reserve's rate cuts. On the other hand, due to tightening Hong Kong dollar liquidity in the banking system during the review period, banks continued to compete for long-term stable deposit funding. Reflecting an increase in the weighted funding cost of Hong Kong dollar deposits, the composite interest rate (a measure of the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks) gradually rose from 0.95% six months earlier to 1.09% at the end of 2019, which remains at a relatively low level by historical standards (green line in Chart 5.3). Chart 5.3 Interest Rates More comprehensively, given that the decline in the USD funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong offset the slight increase in their HKD funding costs, the average overall HKD and USD funding cost for licensed banks in Hong Kong decreased marginally by 14 basis points in the second half of 2019 (Chart 5.4). During the review period, the bank's net interest income benefited from a modest decline in its overall funding costs and from Hong Kong dollar HIBORs remaining at relatively high levels, thereby supporting profitability across the banking sector during the same period. Therefore, figures from June 2019 onwards cannot be directly compared with those of previous months. Looking ahead, several downside risks from both external and domestic environments will continue to cloud banks' profitability outlook. Relevant factors include uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, the trajectory of future China-US trade relations, and escalating geopolitical tensions. An intensification of these risk factors could dampen the already weak momentum of global economic growth and reduce demand for bank credit. Given the broad implementation of accommodative monetary policies by major central banks, the global low-interest-rate environment could persist, potentially exerting pressure on banks' future net interest margins. At the local level, social events that began in mid-2019 continue to weigh on business investment and market confidence. Against a backdrop of an already weakened economic environment, if conditions were to persist or even deteriorate further in the future, credit demand prospects and the quality of banks' asset portfolios could worsen. In terms of overall market development, following the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's issuance of eight virtual banking licenses, Hong Kong banks have begun to launch virtual banking services. The entry of these new market players may increase their market share by offering more convenient products and more attractive deposit rates to attract new customers, which could exert upward pressure on the funding costs of existing banks. While the near-term impact may remain muted given the currently limited scale of virtual banks' operations, their long-term implications could hinge on whether incumbent banks accelerate their adoption of fintech to maintain competitiveness. The results of Theme 5 indicate a statistically significant correlation between the extent to which Hong Kong banks adopt financial technology and improvements in their cost efficiency and profitability. Capitalisation of the Hong Kong banking sector continued to be strong and well above minimum international standards. As of the end of 2019, the consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions (AIs) rose further to 20.7% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio also increased to 18.5%, of which 16.5% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. Chart 5.5 Capitalisation of locally incorporated AIs In addition to the risk-based capital adequacy ratio, Basel III also sets forth a non-risk-based leverage ratio to curb excessive leverage in the banking system. The leverage ratio of locally incorporated AIs stood at a healthy level of 8.2% at the end of 2019, exceeding the statutory minimum of 3% (Figure 5.6). The average LCR of category 1 institutions rose from 152.8% in the second quarter of 2019 to 159.9% in the fourth quarter of 2019 (Chart 5.7), remaining well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Core Funding Ratio of category 2A institutions remained at a high level of 134.5%, exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 75% applicable in 2019. The ample liquidity and sound funding positions of authorized institutions indicate that the Hong Kong banking sector is well positioned to withstand a range of liquidity shocks. Overall, the average loan-to-deposit ratio of all AIs in all currencies increased from 74.5% at the end of June 2019 to 75.4% at the end of that year.
