Amidst heightened US-China trade tensions, a slowing global economy, and ongoing local social events, bank credit growth, which showed a modest rebound in the first half of 2019, slowed down in the second half of the year. On a half-yearly basis, loan growth, measured by the total change in loans and advances of all authorized institutions, increased moderately by 4.2% in the first half of 2019, before slowing to 2.4% in the second half (Chart 5.12). The slowdown in loan growth was attributable to a deceleration in the growth rates of both domestic loans (comprising loans for use in Hong Kong and trade financing) and loans for use outside Hong Kong during the review period. Domestic loans and loans for use outside Hong Kong grew by 2.5% and 2.2% respectively in the second half of 2019, which was lower than the increases of 4.5% and 3.5% recorded in the first half. Nevertheless, the full-year growth in total loans for 2019 moderated to a more moderate increase of 6.7%, up from 4.4% in the full year of 2018.

The rollout of novel coronavirus vaccines has offered hope for economic reopening, boosting global growth prospects. Coupled with sustained fiscal and monetary easing, financial markets have repeatedly reached new highs. However, the global outlook remains clouded by uncertainties, and recovery trajectories across economies are expected to be uneven. In the medium term, the disconnect between financial markets and the real economy, high debt levels, and the long-lasting economic scars left by the pandemic will pose significant challenges for policymakers. The Hong Kong dollar exchange and money markets continued to operate in a smooth and orderly manner. The Hong Kong dollar approached the strong-side convertibility bound, driven primarily by stock-related demand. During the review period, total deposits increased, with no signs of significant outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Partly reflecting weaker economic activity and reduced credit demand due to the resurgence of the pandemic, total bank loans in the second half of the year declined slightly; however, on an annual basis for 2020, they still recorded a modest increase. Meanwhile, the residential property market remained broadly stable. Looking ahead, uncertainties regarding the pace of economic recovery and persistent geopolitical risks will continue to pose challenges to the Hong Kong banking sector. In particular, as the pandemic may undermine the repayment capacity of enterprises and households, the banking sector should remain closely attentive to the impact of related downside risk factors on asset quality. Global economic growth rebounded in the third quarter of 2020 as economies reopened, but with the resurgence of COVID-19 cases from the fourth quarter onwards, global growth slowed once again. Nevertheless, with breakthroughs in vaccine development by the end of 2020, market expectations turned toward the eventual end of the pandemic, paving the way for the global economy to return to normal and accelerate its growth. In addition, sustained fiscal and monetary easing pushed global financial markets to new highs in early 2021, despite emerging signs of decoupling from the real economy. Against this backdrop, uncertainties are expected to continue clouding the global economic outlook. Whether vaccines can be widely distributed remains to be seen. At the same time, supply chain bottlenecks and earlier expansionary monetary policies could push inflation above expectations, prompting central banks to withdraw monetary accommodation sooner than anticipated and thereby overturning financial markets' expectations of a prolonged low-interest-rate regime. In the long term, policymakers need to assess the costs and benefits of extending relief measures and address numerous economic legacies of the pandemic, including elevated global debt levels and lasting economic trauma. In East Asia, domestic GDP growth improved in the second half of 2020, supported by a recovery in export demand. Amid rising risk appetite, regional equity investment inflows recovered, and carry trades re-emerged. Despite the aforementioned positive developments, the East Asia region continues to face persistent uncertainties stemming from the pandemic. First, in the global competition for vaccine procurement, less-developed economies in the region may lag behind advanced economies in achieving herd immunity, hindering the recovery of their tourism and services sectors. Secondly, uncertainties regarding the supply, coverage, or effectiveness of vaccines, combined with a weakening fiscal position of governments in the region, could further dampen market sentiment and trigger capital outflows. As for Mainland China, with consumption activities gradually returning to normal, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020. In 2020 as a whole, the mainland economy grew by 2.3%, making it the only major economy to record positive growth. Looking ahead, the economic outlook remains largely dependent on the trajectory of the pandemic and changes in US-China tensions. The latest consensus forecasts project that the Mainland economy will grow by 8.4% in 2021. The renminbi depreciated for several months at the start of 2020, before strengthening for the remainder of the year amid an accelerating economic recovery, a weaker US dollar, and robust capital inflows into the mainland bond market. Detailed analysis shows that, during the outbreak of the novel coronavirus, fundamental factors—not market sentiment—played a more significant role in driving fluctuations in the RMB exchange rate (see Spotlight 1 for details). The Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020, but real gross domestic product remained well below pre-pandemic levels. With a modest rise in local demand and further expansion in goods exports, seasonally adjusted real GDP began to recover in the third quarter, ending five consecutive quarters of contraction. The year-on-year contraction in real GDP narrowed significantly from 9% in the first half of 2020 to around 3% in the second half. However, in 2020 as a whole, real GDP fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record, marking the first time in history that the economy contracted for two consecutive years following a 1.2% contraction in 2019. Latest data on real GDP across different sectors show that the contraction in consumption- and tourism-related industries has been more severe than that of the overall economy during the pandemic. To address the ongoing pandemic, the Government introduced two additional rounds (the third and fourth) of the Pandemic Relief Fund in the second half of 2020 to support industries and residents affected by the outbreak, while enhancing Hong Kong's epidemic prevention and control capabilities. The Government also announced additional countercyclical measures in the recent 2021/22 Budget to boost the economy, including the issuance of a one-off HK$5,000 electronic consumption voucher and the provision of 100% guaranteed special personal loans for unemployed persons. In collaboration with the SME Banking Loan Coordination Mechanism, the HKMA also announced in March 2021 an extension of the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to October of the same year, and declared an extension of the repayment period for trade finance loans under the Scheme. These deferral measures are expected to help alleviate liquidity constraints faced by some corporate clients. The novel coronavirus vaccine is expected to help restore normal economic activity, with the local economy projected to return to positive growth in 2021 (for the full year). However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery will be influenced by numerous uncertainties, including the trajectory of the pandemic and the rollout progress and effectiveness of the vaccines. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, the local economy is likely to face significant challenges in the first half of 2021. On the external front, Mainland China's economy is expected to strengthen further, providing support for Hong Kong's goods and services exports, while the pace of recovery in other major economies will depend on the effectiveness of their large-scale vaccination programmes. The Government forecasts real GDP growth for 2021 in the range of 3.5% to 5.5%, while the growth estimates from international organizations and private-sector analysts average 4.4%. The labour market situation further deteriorated in the second half of 2020 and the early part of 2021. The unemployment rate continued to climb, reaching a 17-year high of 7.2% in February 2021, while the underemployment rate rose to 4.0%, marking the highest level since the SARS outbreak. To address the deteriorating labour market situation, the Government introduced the "Keep Employees on Payroll" scheme under the second round of the Anti-epidemic Fund, providing time-limited wage subsidies (from June to November 2020) to employers to help them retain their staff. Following the conclusion of the "Employment Support Scheme," the Government introduced additional targeted measures under the third and fourth rounds of the Epidemic Prevention and Control Fund (such as one-off subsidies) to further support industries severely impacted by the pandemic. In the short term, the labor market is expected to remain under pressure due to weak economic conditions. Topic 2 examines the potential impact of the boom and bust in Hong Kong's inbound tourism sector on the local labour market. Local inflationary pressures weakened steadily over the eight-month period from mid-2020 to February 2021. The underlying consumer price index (CPI) inflation rate fell sharply on an annual basis to 0.3% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2020, respectively, and further declined to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February 2021, respectively. The annualized three-month-on-three-month underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, has remained at a low level in recent months despite some slight fluctuations. Given that global and local economic conditions remain challenging, inflationary pressures in Hong Kong are likely to stay mild in the near term. In particular, the moderation in the growth of private residential rents under newly signed leases will continue to restrain domestic inflation. Market consensus forecasts headline inflation in 2021 to be at a moderate 1.4%, while the Government projects underlying and headline inflation rates for 2021 to be 1.0% and 1.6% respectively. The HKD exchange rate against the USD has approached the strong-side convertibility bound, primarily driven by equity-related capital demand, including robust initial public offering (IPO) fundraising activity and southbound capital inflows via the Shanghai-HK Stock Connect and Shenzhen-HK Stock Connect. Fundraising activities remained robust in the first two months of 2021, contributing to a sustained strength in the Hong Kong dollar. During the review period, the strong-side CU was triggered 47 times in September and October 2020, with inflows of HK$263.3 billion. The strong-side conversion facility was triggered a total of 85 times in 2020, with cumulative inflows amounting to HK$383.5 billion. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar markets continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. From a geographical perspective, total deposits increased during the review period, indicating no signs of significant capital outflow from Hong Kong's banking system. Despite uncertainties related to the evolution of the pandemic, the pace of economic recovery, and continued tensions in China-US relations, which may exacerbate volatility in fund flows, Hong Kong possesses ample foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, enabling it to withstand such fluctuations. As the strong-side convertibility guarantee was triggered, leading to an increase in the monetary base, HKD interbank interest rates generally remained at very low levels. Reflecting a decline in retail bank HKD funding costs, the composite interest rate fell further from 0.71% at the end of June 2020 to 0.23% at the end of February 2021. Concurrently, the average lending rate for new mortgages decreased from 2.02% in June to 1.56% in January. On the other hand, the prime lending rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging from 5.00% to 5.50%. As the onshore renminbi (CNY) exchange rate strengthened, the offshore renminbi (CNH) appreciated against the US dollar from late May 2020. Throughout most of the review period, the offshore renminbi exchange rate traded at a premium to the onshore renminbi exchange rate. The average premium in the fourth quarter was approximately 100 basis points, which remains moderate by historical standards. Hong Kong's offshore renminbi (CNH) liquidity pool continued to expand in the second half of 2020, with the total outstanding amount of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit rising to RMB826.3 billion at the end of January 2021. For other renminbi business, renminbi loans by banks in Hong Kong declined, while renminbi trade settlement increased. The average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system remained high at RMB1,191.5 billion throughout 2020. Hong Kong possesses efficient financial infrastructure that offers investors a wide range of cross-border channels for fund flows with the Mainland. With the continued liberalisation of the Mainland's capital account, growing demand from international investors for renminbi-denominated assets, and the deepening of regional economic and financial cooperation under the Belt and Road Initiative and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area Initiative, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit. Supported by gains in global equity markets and active buying of Hong Kong shares by mainland investors via the Stock Connect, the local equity market staged a rebound following a sharp correction at the beginning of the review period. Global equity markets rose, driven by unprecedented monetary easing measures adopted by major economies, optimistic sentiment regarding positive progress in vaccine development—which was expected to accelerate the recovery of economic activity—and a reduction in global geopolitical uncertainties. Against this backdrop, the Hang Seng Index recovered from its sharp decline in 2020, posting a 15.1% increase over the review period and briefly surpassing the 31,000-point level in mid-February 2021, reaching a 32-month high. Supported by stable issuance volumes, the Hong Kong dollar and offshore RMB bond markets continued to expand in the second half of 2020. Following a significant net outflow of capital in the first half of 2020, market confidence rebounded swiftly as governments worldwide implemented unprecedented economic stimulus measures, leading to a recovery in bond fund inflows into the local market. Despite a moderate rebound in bond yields during the same period, global bond yields, including those in Hong Kong, remain near historical lows.

With breakthroughs in vaccine development, markets expect the novel coronavirus pandemic to eventually come to an end, enabling the global economy to accelerate its growth in the years ahead. Amid expectations of a globally accommodative monetary policy regime characterized by "lower rates for longer," investors were not deterred by the late-2020 resurgence of the pandemic, and financial markets reached new highs in early 2021. However, the optimistic outlook in financial markets is at odds with the still-challenging macroeconomic environment. Should economic recovery fall short of expectations or policy support be withdrawn earlier than anticipated (for instance, due to higher-than-expected inflation), asset prices could experience volatility. Looking ahead, policymakers will face the challenge of determining when to withdraw policy support and of addressing a range of lingering pandemic-related issues, including elevated debt levels and long-term economic scars. Continued uncertainty regarding the pandemic continues to cast a shadow over economic recovery in East Asia, with slower-developing emerging market economies in the region likely facing greater challenges in vaccine procurement and distribution. Any slowdown in the progress of vaccination programs could reverse the current optimism, leading to volatile capital flows and financial market instability. As for Mainland China, with consumption activities gradually returning to normal, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020. Looking ahead, the economic growth outlook remains highly uncertain, largely contingent on the trajectory of the pandemic and shifts in US-China tensions. Accordingly, the government announced its continued support for a supportive policy stance and emphasized the importance of controlling systemic risks. Benefiting from the purchasing power released by economic reopening, most major economies recorded better-than-expected real GDP growth in the third quarter of 2020. However, since the fourth quarter, the number of new coronavirus infections has risen again, prompting governments worldwide to reinstate lockdowns and social distancing measures, thereby weakening global growth momentum once more. At the end of 2020, a more transmissible variant of the virus emerged, subsequently spreading globally and exacerbating the situation. Nevertheless, with breakthroughs in vaccine development and the approval of multiple vaccines for use by the end of 2020, markets anticipated that the pandemic would eventually be brought under control, allowing the global economy to return to normal and accelerate its growth. Another driver supporting the global economic recovery has been sustained policy stimulus, including major central banks' commitment to a "lower-for-longer" monetary policy amid weak inflation, as well as continued fiscal easing in major advanced economies, particularly the fiscal stimulus packages enacted by the U.S. Congress in December 2020 and March 2021. Accordingly, in January 2021, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) raised its global real GDP growth forecast for 2021 to 5.5%, an increase of 0.3 percentage points from the projection made in October 2020 (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 IMF Forecasts of Real GDP Growth from January 2021 and October 2020 Against this backdrop, market sentiment improved, with cyclical sectors typically benefiting from economic recovery driving up stock prices, which pushed global equity prices and valuations to record highs in early 2021 (Chart 2.2). Chart 2.2 Twelve-month forward price-to-earnings ratios for major stock indices However, while financial markets have performed robustly, the macroeconomic backdrop remains fraught with challenges; this divergence could lead to volatility in asset markets amid multiple risks. First, the prospect of bringing the epidemic under control depends on whether vaccines can be widely distributed, which remains to be seen. As of mid-March 2021, the global vaccination rate remained low (Chart 2.3). Although global mechanisms such as COVAX have facilitated more equitable vaccine distribution, the low vaccination rates among lower-income emerging market economies are expected to become more severe due to limited vaccine supply. If pandemic control proves suboptimal, various regions may need to maintain social distancing and other restrictive measures, thereby undermining the global recovery outlook. Chart 2.3 Proportion of the population in selected economies who have received at least one dose of a vaccine (as of March 15, 2021) Second, the rebound in financial markets has been underpinned by continued monetary and fiscal policy support, particularly the "lower for longer" monetary policy stance. However, there is a risk that the withdrawal of support measures may proceed faster than expected. For instance, inflation expectations in the US and Europe have risen amid a confluence of supply bottlenecks, robust currency appreciation and liquidity growth, and expansionary fiscal policies (Figure 2.4). Should future inflation prove stronger than expected, central banks may need to scale back monetary easing, while inflation data exceeding expectations could also lead to heightened volatility in financial markets. Figure 2.4: US and Euro Area 5y5y Inflation-Linked Swap Rates. Third, significant uncertainties remain in future China–US relations. The trend of US-China decoupling, particularly in the financial and technology sectors, has intensified since the outbreak of the pandemic. Given that both the Democratic and Republican parties in the United States have adopted increasingly hardline stances toward Mainland China, this trend is unlikely to reverse under the Biden administration. Should US-China relations unexpectedly escalate, it could trigger financial market turbulence in the future. Looking ahead, policymakers will need to grapple with the difficult question of whether and when to withdraw pandemic support measures. While withdrawing such measures prematurely could jeopardize economic recovery and trigger a "cliff effect," in the long run, the costs of maintaining them are substantial. These include imposing a fiscal burden and delaying the necessary post-pandemic reallocation of resources—for instance, allowing "zombie enterprises," whose business models are no longer viable, to survive through continued government support. Furthermore, policymakers must also address the numerous challenges left in the wake of the pandemic. First, global debt levels surged in 2020 due to declining corporate revenues and a sharp increase in government spending (Figure 2.5). Although the sharp rise in debt is not immediately problematic given that global interest rates are currently at historically low levels, the continued accumulation of debt in both the public and private sectors could fuel concerns about fiscal sustainability and financial stability. Figure 2.5 Global debt-to-GDP ratio. Another lingering issue concerns the potential long-term economic losses or lasting scars that the pandemic may inflict. For instance, heightened uncertainty may cause firms to cut investment, while workers long affected by unemployment may permanently exit the labor market, resulting in significant waste of human resources. In East Asia, real GDP growth plummeted in the second quarter of 2020 before stabilizing in the latter half of the year (Chart 2.6). The momentum of the economic recovery has been driven primarily by a rebound in exports, with particularly strong demand for electronics and technical equipment. At the same time, the hardest-hit service sectors—such as tourism and consumer services that require face-to-face interaction with customers—continue to struggle. Chart 2.6 East Asia: 2020 Real GDP Growth Despite ongoing uncertainties surrounding the economic recovery, portfolio investment funds have resumed inflows. Since the second half of last year, improved market sentiment and higher yields relative to advanced economy bonds have attracted greater bond capital inflows into the region (Chart 2.7). Amidst signs of economic recovery and the rollout of vaccine production programs, equity fund flows into East Asia accelerated in the final quarter of 2020. Regional currencies also appreciated in response to equity capital inflows, prompting a rebound of approximately 10% in the Bloomberg J.P. Morgan Asia Dollar Index from its low in March of the previous year. Chart 2.7 East Asia: Portfolio Investment Flows The East Asia region continues to face persistent uncertainties arising from the pandemic. First, although the rollout of vaccines has brought hope to the region's severely impacted service sectors and economies, global competition for early vaccine supplies has driven up procurement costs, while vaccine distribution has posed challenges to the region's logistics and public health capacities. Therefore, slower-developing economies in the region may achieve herd immunity later than advanced economies, and uneven vaccination rates across economies could prolong border closures and delay the recovery of tourism-related sectors. Second, as investor optimism has been largely driven by the rollout of vaccines, any significant shortfall in the pace or effectiveness of vaccination could bring an end to the current capital inflows and the rebound in financial asset prices. A sharp reduction in capital inflows could trigger another wave of market turbulence. With the successful containment of the novel coronavirus and a gradual rebound in consumption, the Mainland economy experienced a rapid recovery in the second half of 2020. Meanwhile, exports also maintained growth, buoyed by strong demand for pandemic-related products such as medical equipment and high-tech goods (Figure 2.8). Looking back at 2020, despite the unprecedented impact of the novel coronavirus pandemic on the economy, Mainland China's GDP still recorded growth of 2.3%. Chart 2.8 Mainland China: Contribution to GDP growth by demand component Looking ahead, the latest consensus forecast indicates that Mainland China's economy will grow robustly by 8.4% in 2021, with private consumption expected to emerge as the primary driver of economic growth. However, whether the economic recovery can be sustained will, to some extent, continue to depend on the trajectory of the pandemic. Although industrial production activity in mainland China has normalized, the service sector remains partially disrupted as outbreaks have re-emerged in several northern provinces. Regarding the external environment, although exports resumed growth in the second half of 2020, global demand remained uncertain due to a new wave of the pandemic in most developed economies. Furthermore, tensions between China and the United States are unlikely to ease in the short term; however, the recently signed Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) and the agreed-upon China-EU Comprehensive Agreement on Investment may facilitate China's deeper integration with other economies, potentially offsetting some of the adverse effects of US-China decoupling on economic recovery. Given the continued uncertainty surrounding the economic outlook, the Central Economic Work Conference held in December 2020 announced that existing policy stances would remain largely unchanged in 2021 to support economic growth, while also emphasizing the importance of managing systemic risks, such as maintaining macro leverage stability and ensuring the sustainability of local government debt. Additionally, the latest government work report set the growth target for 2021 at over 6%. In the long term, the 14th Five-Year Plan designates technological self-reliance and self-strengthening and the dual circulation strategy as priority development directions, aiming to raise per capita GDP to the level of a moderately developed country by 2035. The impact of the novel coronavirus outbreak on the debt repayment capacity of issuers appears to have been limited, with the overall default rate in the Mainland bond market remaining at a low level in the second half of 2020. However, due to a significant surge in state-owned enterprise bond defaults, the total amount of defaulted bonds increased in 2020 (Chart 2.9). While the rise in defaults by state-owned enterprises mainly reflects the central government's resolve to break the "implicit guarantee" of such enterprises and promote more rational market risk pricing, constrained fiscal space for some local governments may also be a contributing factor, particularly in less developed regions. Chart 2.9 Mainland China: Onshore Bond Default Volumes and Proportions In the second half of 2020, financing costs for corporate issuers rose, particularly for some high-risk issuers. Despite the continued economic recovery and the gradual normalization of interest rates, which contributed to rising financing costs for lower-rated issuers, several corporate default incidents in the fourth quarter of 2020 led to a significant widening of credit spreads (Figure 2.10). Chart 2.10 Mainland China: Yields on 5-year corporate bonds On the property market front, housing prices in the Mainland continued to rise in the second half of 2020, particularly in first-tier cities. In contrast, the pace of house price appreciation in lower-tier cities was significantly slower (Chart 2.11). In previous years, the oversupply of housing in third-tier cities posed a significant challenge; however, this issue was largely brought under control by 2020, partly due to robust sales driven by buoyant market sentiment in those cities. As of the end of 2020, the inventory-to-sales ratio in tier-3 cities remained at approximately 13 months, significantly lower than the peak of 31 months recorded in early 2015.

Although real GDP remained well below pre-pandemic levels, Hong Kong's economy improved in the second half of 2020, as domestic demand recovered and exports of goods expanded further. Anticipating a return of economic activity to normality following the rollout of COVID-19 vaccinations, Hong Kong's economy is expected to resume growth in 2021 after contracting by its steepest rate on record in 2020. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery are influenced by numerous uncertainties, including the evolution of the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, the Hong Kong economy is likely to face significant challenges in early 2021. Therefore, labour markets are expected to remain under pressure in the short term, while local inflationary pressures will stay moderate. The Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020 (Table 3.A), but economic activity remained well below pre-pandemic levels. The year-on-year decline in real GDP narrowed to 3.6% in the third quarter and further narrowed to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. However, in 2020 as a whole, real GDP fell by 6.1%, marking the largest decline on record and representing the first instance of two consecutive years of contraction since a 1.2% shrinkage in 2019. Latest data on Gross Domestic Product (GDP) by industry also show that economic activities in the vast majority of sectors contracted on an annual basis over recent quarters, with declines in consumption- and tourism-related sectors being more pronounced than the overall economy. On a quarter-on-quarter basis, real GDP began to recover from the third quarter of 2020, ending five consecutive quarters of decline (Table 3.A and Chart 3.1). Local private consumption resumed positive growth in both the third and fourth quarters. However, amid the third and fourth waves of the local pandemic, the authorities reimposed social distancing measures, and consumer confidence remained weak. With a brief rebound in business sentiment, overall investment spending also increased in the second half of the year. Partly benefiting from a stronger export performance, particularly exports to mainland China, Hong Kong's goods trade expanded further (Figure 3.2). With the global tourism industry still stagnating, trade in services remained weak. Overall, net imports (trade deficit) weighed down GDP in the second half of the year, partly reflecting a slower rebound in goods exports compared to imports. Figure 3.1: Growth Rate of Real GDP and Contributions from Major Expenditure Components  Figure 3.2: Real Exports and Imports  In response to the ongoing pandemic, the Government introduced two additional rounds (the third and fourth rounds) of the Pandemic Prevention and Control Fund, totalling HK$30.4 billion, between September and December 2020, to assist industries and residents affected by the epidemic and to enhance Hong Kong's pandemic prevention and control capabilities. The Government also announced additional countercyclical measures in the recent 2021/22 Budget to boost the economy, including issuing one-off electronic consumption vouchers of HK$5,000 and providing fully guaranteed special personal loans for unemployed persons. The HKMA, together with the SME Loan Coordination Mechanism of the Banking Sector, also announced in March 2021 a further extension of the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to October of the same year, and declared an extension of the repayment period for trade finance loans under the Scheme. These deferral measures are expected to help alleviate liquidity constraints faced by some corporate clients. The rollout of COVID-19 vaccines is expected to restore economic activity to normal, with Hong Kong's economy projected to return to positive growth in 2021 on a full-year basis. However, the pace and strength of the economic recovery remain subject to numerous uncertainties, including the evolution of the pandemic, the pace of vaccine deployment, and its effectiveness. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, the local economy will continue to face significant challenges in the first half of 2021. On the external front, China's economy is expected to further strengthen, providing support for Hong Kong's exports of goods and services. Meanwhile, the recovery pace of other major economies will depend on the effectiveness of their large-scale vaccination programs, which in turn will affect Hong Kong's goods trade and inbound tourism. The Government forecasts real GDP growth for the whole of 2021 in the range of 3.5% to 5.5%, while growth estimates from international organizations and private-sector analysts average 4.4%. The labour market situation further deteriorated in the second half of 2020 and the early part of 2021. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose further to 7.2% in February 2021, reaching its highest level in 17 years (Chart 3.3). The underemployment rate also rose to 4.0%, marking the highest level since the SARS outbreak. Total employment stabilized after declining to a low level (Chart 3.3), while government data indicate that the number of job vacancies continued to fall. The nominal average earnings index for employed persons, which reflects labor income, decelerated to 2.0% in the third quarter of 2020, marking the lowest growth rate in nearly 11 years. To address the deteriorating labour market situation, the Government introduced the "Keep Employment" scheme under the second round of the Epidemic Prevention and Relief Fund, providing time-limited wage subsidies (from June to November 2020) to employers to help them retain their staff. Following the conclusion of the "Employment Support Scheme", the Government introduced additional targeted measures under the third and fourth rounds of the Epidemic Prevention and Control Fund (such as one-off subsidies) to further support industries severely impacted by the pandemic. In the near term, the labor market is expected to remain under pressure due to weak economic conditions. Topic 2 examines the potential impact of the boom and bust in Hong Kong's inbound tourism sector on the local labour market. Chart 3.3 Labour market conditions Chart 3.4 Different measures of consumer price inflation Local inflationary pressures continued to ease over the eight-month period from mid-2020 to February 2021. The underlying consumer price index inflation rate declined significantly on an annual basis to 0.3% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2020, respectively, and further fell to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February 2021, respectively (Figure 3.4). The annualised three-month-on-three-month underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, experienced some fluctuations in recent months but remained at a low level. Specifically, price pressures on staple foods have eased, and the cost of dining out has declined noticeably, reflecting that more restaurants have offered delivery discounts during periods when dine-in services were restricted. Price pressures for other traded goods (such as durable goods) are likely to remain moderate. In the services sector, amid the consolidation of private residential rents, the rental component of the Composite Consumer Price Index remained weak (Chart 3.5). Labour cost pressures also eased in recent quarters (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.5 CCPI rental component and market rents Chart 3.6 Unit labour cost Given that global and local economic conditions remain challenging, inflationary pressures in Hong Kong are expected to remain mild in the near term. Particularly due to the recent slowdown in rent growth for newly signed private residential leases, local inflation will continue to be contained. Market consensus forecasts the headline inflation rate for 2021 to be a moderate 1.4%, while the Government projects the underlying inflation rate to be 1% and the headline inflation rate to be 1.6%. As the novel coronavirus pandemic swept across, Hong Kong's tourism industry rapidly fell into decline, sparking market concerns that the crisis could inflict a scarring effect on the future recovery of the labor market. To this end, this special empirical study examines the impact of a thriving inbound tourism sector on Hong Kong's labor market, thereby exploring the potential consequences of the current downturn in the tourism industry. Since 2000, Hong Kong's tourism sector has experienced significant volatility (Chart B2.1). Specifically, visitor arrivals to Hong Kong declined during the 2003 SARS (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome) outbreak. Since the introduction of the Individual Visit Scheme (independent travel) in July of the same year, visitor arrivals began to surge. Under the original individual visit scheme, mainland residents could apply as individuals for one to two visits per year, with each stay not exceeding seven days. The Individual Visit Scheme was expanded starting from April 2009, allowing eligible residents with Shenzhen household registration to apply for a "One Visit, Multiple Entries" visa for multiple visits to Hong Kong within a one-year period. Since then, the number of tourist arrivals from the Mainland has surged. Driven by new cross-boundary infrastructure projects connecting Hong Kong and Mainland China, visitor arrivals to Hong Kong reached a record high between late 2018 and early 2019. Subsequent local social events in the second half of 2019 led to a halving of visitor arrivals, while the novel coronavirus pandemic has further left Hong Kong's tourism sector in a state of stagnation since the end of January 2020. Figure B2.1: Tourist Arrivals and Relevant Policies Using the example of the influx of tourism driven by the Individual Visit Scheme, we examine the impact of inbound tourism on local employment and income. We consider the individual visit scheme introduced in 2003 to be akin to a random economic shock, as its timing was nearly exogenous and unforeseeable to local residents. Our primary analytical data are drawn from population statistics collected through Hong Kong's Population Census and Mid-term Population Census. Specifically, we utilized 5% samples from the censuses or mid-term population censuses conducted in 1996, 2001, 2006, 2011, and 2016. In addition, we also define tourism-related sectors as catering, retail, accommodation, and transportation. First, we adopt a difference-in-differences framework to compare the employment outcomes before and after the implementation of the Individual Visit Scheme between the treatment group, comprising young workers aged 20–40, and the control group, consisting of older workers aged 41–65. We assigned the younger group to the "treatment group" because they are at the early stage of their careers and can more flexibly make significant adjustments to their employment decisions in response to exogenous growth in inbound tourism. As the impact of the thriving tourism sector driven by the Individual Visit Scheme on the labor market may evolve over time, we also employ an event study approach to identify time-varying effects. Our empirical results indicate that, compared with older groups, younger workers (particularly women and those with only secondary education) were more likely to enter tourism-related industries following the implementation of the Individual Visit Scheme. Among these, the Individual Visit Scheme had a particularly pronounced and lasting impact on the likelihood of young women entering tourism-related occupations, maintaining a level close to 5 percentage points higher than the average entry probability for older age groups since 2006 (Figure B2.2). We also employ a similar approach to compare the income of sectors engaged in tourism-related activities (treatment group) with those not engaged in such activities (control group). Estimation results indicate that following the implementation of the Individual Visit Scheme, employees working in tourism-related sectors experienced higher income growth compared to those in non-tourism sectors. Furthermore, compared with similar employees in other sectors, female workers and those with lower educational qualifications in the tourism-related industries experienced higher and rising income growth rates, ranging from 3 to 20 percentage points (Figure B2.3). Figure B2.2 Impact of the Individual Visit Scheme on Female Employment  Figure B2.3 Impact of the Individual Visit Scheme on the Incomes of Women and Workers with Lower Educational Attainment  These findings are broadly consistent with international experience, highlighting that the tourism sector is a significant source of employment, particularly for young people, women, and workers with lower levels of education. In the case of Hong Kong, our findings are also consistent with previous analyses, indicating that the strong growth in inbound tourism has increased demand for lower-skilled workers, thereby enhancing the resilience of the lower-skilled labour market. As the inbound tourism sector in Hong Kong has declined from a period of prosperity to a trough, these groups of workers may be more adversely affected, warranting close monitoring.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate continued to stay close to the strong-side convertibility guarantee, which was triggered multiple times between September and October 2020. Strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar was mainly driven by stock-related funding needs, including robust new share issuance activities and net inflows through the Shanghai-HK and Shenzhen-HK Stock Connect schemes. As the surplus balance increased to over HKD 450 billion, HIBORs declined across the board. Despite uncertainties related to the evolution of the COVID-19 pandemic, the pace of economic recovery, and ongoing tensions between China and the United States, which may exacerbate volatility in fund flows, Hong Kong possesses ample foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, enabling it to withstand the pressures arising from such fund flow fluctuations. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate hovered near the strong-side convertibility guarantee, primarily driven by equity-related funding demand, including robust new share issuance activities and southbound capital inflows via the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect (Figure 4.1). Although some funds raised through initial public offerings were transferred out, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained within a narrow range of 7.7505 to 7.7544 during November and December, supported by improved sentiment in the local stock market and market expectations of rising funding demand as year-end approached. With fundraising activity remaining robust in the first two months of 2021 (Chart 4.2), the HKD/USD exchange rate closed at 7.7568 on February 26, 2021. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to proceed in a smooth and orderly manner. During the review period, the strong exchange rate guarantee was triggered on multiple occasions, leading to an increase in the overall outstanding amount and reflecting substantial capital inflows into the Hong Kong dollar. From September to October 2020, the strong-side conversion guarantee was triggered 47 times. Under the design of the linked exchange rate system, the Exchange Fund sold a total of HK$263.3 billion, raising the aggregate balance from HK$193.1 billion at the end of August to HK$457.5 billion at the end of February (Chart 4.3). The strong-side conversion guarantee was triggered a total of 85 times in 2020, with cumulative inflows amounting to HK$383.5 billion. From a cross-border perspective, the increase in total deposits indicates no signs of significant capital outflow from Hong Kong's banking system. At the same time, the latest balance of payments data indicate that direct investment by non-residents continued to flow into Hong Kong in the fourth quarter of 2020, with no signs of abnormal capital movements. Chart 4.1 Hong Kong Dollar Exchange Rate  Chart 4.2 Equity Capital Raised on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange (HKEX)  Chart 4.3 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes (EFBNs)  During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER) broadly followed the weakening of the US dollar against major currencies and declined (Chart 4.4). Given that the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners remained narrow and had limited impact on the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index (REER), the REER trend generally followed that of the nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER). Chart 4.4 NEER and REER Looking ahead, uncertainties related to the pandemic trajectory, the pace of economic recovery, and sustained tensions in China–US relations may heighten fund-flow volatility. As an international financial centre, Hong Kong hosts a wide range of fundraising activities, such as new share offerings, resulting in substantial capital inflows and outflows. On the one hand, relevant fundraising activities can attract international investors to channel funds into Hong Kong. On the other hand, funds raised by listed companies may subsequently be diverted away from Hong Kong to meet business needs. Hong Kong possesses ample foreign reserves and a sound banking system, enabling it to withstand fluctuations in capital flows without compromising financial stability. Amid continued inflows of Hong Kong dollar funds, the local monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2020 and in recent months. In the eight-month period since end-June 2020, the Hong Kong dollar monetary base increased by 20.8% (Chart 4.5). By component, the increase in the monetary base during this period was primarily due to the multiple triggers of the strong-side convertibility guarantee, which led to a rise in the aggregate balance. On the other hand, other components, including Deposit Certificates, government-issued circulating banknotes and coins, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Bonds, remained relatively stable. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base. During the review period, large-scale IPO fundraising activities led to an increase in Hong Kong dollar deposits arising from IPO subscription loans, resulting in a significant rise in Hong Kong dollar broad money (HK M3) and its Hong Kong dollar deposit component between July and October 2020 and in January 2021 (Chart 4.6). Following the conclusion of new share fundraising activities and the repayment of subscription loans by clients, HKD deposits and broad money returned to normal levels by the end of 2020. In January 2021, Hong Kong dollar M3 rose sharply again, primarily driven by large-scale IPO fundraising activities at the end of the month. Overall, Hong Kong dollar M3 grew by 21.7% over the seven-month period since end-June; excluding the impact of the share issuance activities at the end of January, Hong Kong dollar M3 increased modestly by 9.1%. Based on an analysis of the corresponding assets, excluding new share subscription loans, the growth in HKD M3 was primarily driven by an increase in the monetary base triggered by the Strong Side Convertibility. As a major component of Hong Kong dollar M3, HKD deposits rose by 22.9% during the same period. Excluding the impact of the share issuance activities at the end of January, HKD deposits increased moderately by 9.1%. Although term deposits in Hong Kong dollars declined due to low interest rates, this was fully offset by a rapid increase in demand deposits and savings deposits, driven in part by investment demand. Chart 4.6 Deposits by currency held by authorized institutions; Chart 4.7 Changes in HKD M3 and corresponding assets. Total foreign currency deposits increased steadily by 3.6% over the seven-month period since end-June. USD deposits edged down by 0.3%, partly reflecting the weakness of the US dollar, while deposits in other foreign currencies rose robustly by 15.5% during the same period, primarily driven by an increase in RMB deposits. Overall, due to short-term volatility in Hong Kong dollar deposits triggered by initial public offering (IPO) fundraising activities, total deposits with authorized institutions rose sharply by 13.2% during the review period (Chart 4.6). Excluding the share capital-raising activities at the end of January, total deposits increased modestly by 6.4%. It should be noted that monthly monetary statistics may fluctuate due to various short-term factors, such as seasonal trends, funding demands related to initial public offerings (IPOs), and business and investment activities; therefore, these statistics should be interpreted with caution. With the increase in the settlement balance, the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) remained at a very low level overall during the review period (Chart 4.8). Although there was a large-scale new share issuance activity in the second half of 2020, Hong Kong interbank offered rates (HIBORs) did not experience significant volatility due to ample liquidity in the banking system. Overall, Hong Kong's interbank market continued to operate normally. Chart 4.8 HKD and USD interbank HIBOR The HKD yield curve broadly followed the trend of the USD yield curve, steepening during the review period as short-term bond yields declined while long-term bond yields rose (Chart 4.9). Compared to late June, the yield on the 3-year Hong Kong Government Bond declined slightly by 4 basis points to 0.23% by late February, while the yield on the 10-year Hong Kong Government Bond rose by 67 basis points to 1.30% over the same period. Chart 4.9 Government bond yields, composite interest rates, and average new mortgage lending rates Retail-level HKD interest rates have mainly declined in line with the fall in the HKD interbank interest rates. The composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of HKD funds for retail banks, fell further to 0.23% by the end of February 2021 from 0.71% at the end of June 2021 (Chart 4.9). Due to a reduction in funding costs, the average lending rate for new mortgages also declined from 2.02% in June 2020 to 1.56% in January 2021, broadly following the trend of the one-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR). On the other hand, the Best Lending Rates offered by retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging from 5.00% to 5.50%. Under the Linked Exchange Rate System, Hong Kong dollar interest rates are influenced by US dollar interest rates. Given that US interest rates have remained low for an extended period, HKD interest rates are expected to continue at low levels, with intermittent fluctuations driven by capital market activity and seasonal liquidity demands. Against the backdrop of an highly uncertain macro-financial environment, the ample liquidity in the banking system should provide sufficient buffers to maintain Hong Kong's monetary and financial stability. The offshore renminbi (CNH) and onshore renminbi (CNY) exchange rates against the US dollar have strengthened since the end of May 2024 (Chart 4.10), broadly reflecting more favorable economic prospects in Mainland China relative to the rest of the world, alongside a weaker US dollar. FTSE Russell announced in late September that mainland China government bonds would be included in the Global Government Bond Index, further bolstering demand for the renminbi and supporting its appreciation. Throughout most of the review period, the offshore RMB exchange rate traded at a premium to the onshore RMB rate. The average premium in the fourth quarter was approximately 100 basis points, which remains moderate by historical standards. Figure 4.10 Onshore and offshore RMB exchange rates: Liquidity conditions in the offshore renminbi (CNH) interbank market remained stable during the review period. While the overnight CNH HIBOR experienced brief fluctuations due to occasional northbound remittance demands and seasonal liquidity needs approaching the year-end, it mostly remained below 4% (Chart 4.11). The three-month offshore renminbi (CNH) Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) declined in late December, following onshore renminbi rates, before rising again in late January, partly due to tighter onshore liquidity and seasonal factors. Chart 4.11 Overnight and 3-month offshore renminbi (CNH) HIBOR fixings In the second half of 2020, Hong Kong's CNH liquidity pool continued to grow. Since the fourth quarter, the growth rate of renminbi deposits has accelerated, partly reflecting the appreciation of the renminbi and its relatively higher interest rates compared with other currencies. Compared with the end of June 2020, the growth rate of the outstanding balance of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit accelerated, reaching RMB826.3 billion at the end of January 2021, a 21.9% increase (Chart 4.12 and Table 4.A). Among the total, RMB customer deposits grew by 24.7%, primarily driven by strong growth in corporate customer deposits. On the other hand, the outstanding amount of certificates of deposit (CDs) decreased by 25.0% over the same period. Chart 4.12 Renminbi deposits and certificates of deposit in Hong Kong For other renminbi business, the outstanding amount of renminbi loans declined by 2.4% to RMB159.2 billion over the seven-month period since the end of June 2020. On the other hand, Hong Kong's renminbi trade settlement continued to grow robustly. Transactions handled by banks in Hong Kong amounted to RMB3,769.5 billion during the seven-month period from July 2020 to January 2021, an increase of 16.7% compared with the same period of the previous year. In the related transactions, outward remittances to the Mainland from Hong Kong grew at a higher rate than inward remittances to Hong Kong from the Mainland (Chart 4.13). Hong Kong possesses a deep renminbi liquidity pool, sufficient to continue supporting a large volume of renminbi payments and financial transactions. For 2020 as a whole, the average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system reached RMB1,191.5 billion, up from RMB1,133.9 billion in 2019.

Due to the persistent economic downturn triggered by recurrent waves of the novel coronavirus pandemic, compounded by the prolonged low-interest-rate environment, retail banks in Hong Kong saw their profits decline further in the second half of 2020, while asset quality also deteriorated slightly. Nevertheless, the Hong Kong banking sector remained robust, supported by its strong capital and liquidity positions. During the review period, to continue supporting the overall economy in navigating through challenges, the HKMA decided to extend several relief measures. Looking ahead, although the rollout of vaccines offers hope that the global pandemic can be brought under control and economic activities can resume, the pace of economic recovery remains uncertain. These uncertainties, coupled with persistent geopolitical tensions, will be detrimental to business activity and continue to pose challenges for Hong Kong's banking sector. In particular, the pandemic may undermine the repayment capacity of corporations and households; therefore, the banking sector should continue to closely monitor the impact of relevant downside risk factors on asset quality. In the second half of 2020, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks declined by 38.5% compared with the same period in 2019. Accordingly, the return on assets fell to 0.62% in the second half of 2020, compared with 1.13% in the same period of 2019 (Chart 5.1). The net interest margin of retail banks narrowed from 1.63% in the second half of 2019 to 1.01% in the same period of 2020 (Chart 5.2), leading to a decline in net interest income that exceeded the modest growth in non-interest income, resulting in lower profitability. For the full year of 2020, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 29.4%, while return on assets declined from 1.19% in 2019 to 0.77%. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Largely due to significant capital inflows driven by stock market activity, Hong Kong dollar liquidity has become more abundant. Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates softened further in the fourth quarter of 2020. Among them, the three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) declined by 43 basis points in the second half to 0.35% at the end of 2020 (blue line in Chart 5.3). The trend in the composite interest rate (a measure of the average cost of HKD funds for retail banks) was also broadly similar, declining sharply from 0.71% at the end of June 2020 to 0.28% at the end of 2020 (green line in Chart 5.3). The overall decline in interest rates primarily reflects lower interbank funding costs and rate reductions on time deposits by some major retail banks. Chart 5.3 Interest Rates More broadly, the overall average HKD and USD funding cost for licensed banks in Hong Kong declined moderately by 53 basis points during the second half of 2020 (red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and maturity profiles of licensed banks Looking ahead, given that the global low-interest-rate environment is likely to persist and continue to weigh on banks' net interest margin performance, the profitability outlook for the banking sector remains challenging. Furthermore, despite breakthroughs in vaccine development that have bolstered market optimism regarding the global economic outlook, the trajectory of economic recovery remains highly uncertain due to significant uncertainties surrounding vaccine distribution and efficacy. The aforementioned risk factors are likely to continue affecting the asset quality and profitability of the banking sector in the near term. Capitalisation of the Hong Kong banking sector continued to be strong and well above minimum international standards. The consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions (AIs) stood at 20.7% as of the end of December 2020, well above the international minimum requirement of 8% (Chart 5.5). During the period, the Tier 1 capital ratio was 18.7%, of which 16.7% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. In addition, the leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions stood at a healthy level of 8.2% at the end of December 2020, exceeding the statutory minimum of 3% (Figure 5.6). Chart 5.5 Capitalisation of locally incorporated AIs Chart 5.6 Leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions The liquidity positions of the banking sector, as measured by the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR), remained sound during the review period. The average LCR of category 1 institutions was 155.1% in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Chart 5.7), remaining well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. During the same period, the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (LMR) of category 2 institutions was 57.9%, also well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio The latest ratios under the Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) requirement also reflected a stable funding position of AIs. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) of category 1 institutions and the average Core Capital Ratio of category 2A institutions remained at high levels of 138.6% and 139.5%, respectively, in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Chart 5.8), well above their respective statutory minimum requirements of 100% and 75%. The ample liquidity and sound funding positions of authorized institutions indicate that the Hong Kong banking sector is well positioned to withstand liquidity shocks. At the end of 2020, the share of customer deposits to all AIs' total liabilities remained stable at 56.1%, roughly unchanged from six months earlier (Chart 5.9). The total deposit balance increase largely reflected growth in both Hong Kong dollar and foreign currency deposits. Accordingly, at the end of 2020, the average HKD and foreign-currency loan-to-deposit ratios declined to 83.5% and 61.0%, respectively, compared with 86.4% and 65.5% six months earlier. Chart 5.10 Average loan-to-deposit ratios of all AIs The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained at a relatively low level in the fourth quarter of 2020. Under a hypothetical shock of an across-the-board 200-basis-point increase in Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rates, the economic value of locally incorporated licensed banks' interest rate positions is estimated to decline by an amount equivalent to 1.41% of their total capital base at the end of December 2020 (Figure 5.11). However, for the full year of 2020, total bank lending still recorded positive growth, albeit with a significant slowdown from 6.7% in 2019 to 1.2%. On a half-yearly basis, after a 3.0% increase in the first half of 2020, total loans and advances of all AIs declined by 1.8% in the second half (Chart 5.12). After a sharp increase of 10.6% in the first half of 2020, foreign currency loans declined by 4.5% in the second half, partly reflecting a reduction in demand for US dollar loans as global liquidity conditions improved. Banks' outlook for short-term credit demand has improved slightly compared to six months ago. According to the results of the HKMA Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook in December 2020, the share of surveyed AIs expecting loan demand to increase in the next three months rose to 37%, while the share expecting loan demand to decline in the same period fell to 13% (Table 5.A). Due to the adverse impact of the pandemic on the repayment capacity of households and corporations, the asset quality of bank loans deteriorated slightly, yet remained robust by both historical and international standards. Furthermore, the pace of deterioration in loan quality also slowed in the second half of 2020. The gross classified loan ratio (CLR) of all AIs eased upward to 0.9% by the end of 2020 from 0.79% six months prior, while the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans of all AIs increased from 0.49% at the end of June 2020 to 0.57% by the end of 2020. The novel coronavirus pandemic caused a major shock to global financial markets in March 2020. During this period of market turbulence, certain open-ended funds experienced substantial outflows (Figure B1.1), placing pressure on their liquidity management. Figure B1.1: Net outflows from select open-ended funds during the March 2020 episode. In addition to investors' liquidity needs, a further driver of substantial outflows may have been investors' adoption of a "first-mover advantage" strategy, redeeming their funds early to avoid potentially sharp increases in redemption costs under stressed market conditions. To curb capital outflows driven by first-mover advantage, certain open-ended funds have adopted swing pricing—a pricing mechanism for open-ended funds that mitigates the first-mover advantage for investors. Although many open-ended funds employed swing pricing during this event, there is no empirical evidence indicating whether swing pricing effectively reduces outflows from open-ended funds. Against this backdrop, this study conducts an empirical investigation to determine whether swing pricing during the March 2020 episode could have mitigated outflows from open-ended funds, thereby reducing their liquidity risk. Additionally, this report will also identify factors that may limit the effectiveness of swing pricing during periods of market stress. Based on these assessments, we will propose policy recommendations on financial stability. First-mover advantage refers to investors redeeming their investments earlier than others, thereby shifting the redemption costs onto them. First-mover advantages are primarily observed in open-ended funds that adhere to traditional pricing rules, whereby the subscription and redemption costs incurred by investors (such as transaction costs arising from portfolio adjustments) are reflected in the open-ended fund's price only after the transaction is executed. Under this pricing mechanism, the first investors redeeming shares will not bear such transaction costs. This has become an incentive for them to redeem their funds early, particularly when large redemption costs are anticipated. Therefore, during periods of market stress, the first-mover advantage becomes more pronounced as the expected cost of redemptions rises. This amplifies redemption pressures and liquidity risks facing open-ended funds.

Major global stock markets continued to rise in the fourth quarter of 2021; however, amid growing concerns over the tightening stance of central banks in advanced economies and the escalating Russia-Ukraine conflict, major stock markets have since corrected from January 2022 onwards. Global risks and the uncertainty surrounding the trajectory of Hong Kong's pandemic outbreak pushed the Hang Seng Index to a near two-year low in late February. At the same time, the Hong Kong offshore RMB bond market continued to grow steadily in the second half of 2021. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impacts of the relevant risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios.
