Climate change affects all aspects of life, and every individual has a responsibility to contribute to mitigating its impacts. In this regard, the HKMA has invested substantial efforts in advancing Hong Kong's climate goals and contributing to enhancing global climate resilience and sustainable development. Following last year's decision to include our inaugural Sustainability Report as a chapter within the HKMA's 2021 Annual Report, we are, for the first time this year, publishing the 2022 Sustainability Report as a standalone document. I hope this report enables readers to gain a deeper understanding of the Monetary Authority's strategies and priorities in enhancing the Hong Kong banking sector's capacity to address climate change, building a green finance ecosystem, and implementing its role as a responsible investor and sustainable development institution. During the year, we made significant progress in advancing the sustainable development work across the key functions of the Monetary Authority. Readers will learn from this report our specific measures and initiatives, with a particular focus on the following: banks' day-to-day operations are exposed to climate risks. As the banking regulator, the HKMA has taken concrete measures to enhance the banking sector's capacity to respond to climate change. In 2022, we formulated a two-year plan to integrate climate risk factors into regulatory processes and to explore how technology can assist banks in assessing the impact of physical risks. Recognizing that banks are launching an increasing array of green and sustainable products, we have also shared industry best practices on effectively managing these products to enhance banks' capacity for climate risk management. The Monetary Authority is actively engaged in various cooperative initiatives aimed at addressing climate risks and promoting the development of sustainable finance. Locally, we are collaborating with other financial regulators through the Cross-Institutional Steering Group on Green and Sustainable Finance (the Steering Group) to develop a local green taxonomy. This taxonomy will enhance transparency in financial markets and foster greater coherence in green finance policies. At the international level, we are actively engaging with various international organizations to help shape climate change policies and assess their impact on financial stability. Hong Kong is well-positioned to meet Asia's demand for green and sustainable financing. Despite 2022 being a challenging year for the global bond market, green and sustainable debt issuance in Hong Kong continued to post robust growth, rising by 42% to reach a total of US$80.5 billion, cementing its position as the largest centre in Asia for international green and sustainable bond issuances. Relevant issuers include the Shenzhen Municipal People's Government and the Hainan Provincial People's Government, whose bond issuances further underscore Hong Kong's unique role in facilitating green and sustainable capital flows between the Mainland and the international community. The robust development of Hong Kong's green bond market is also partly attributable to the Government Green Bond Programme. Since 2019, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) has assisted the Government in issuing green bonds with a total value of nearly US$16 billion. The proceeds have been allocated to over 40 green government projects, including green buildings, waste management and resource recycling, energy efficiency, and energy conservation. We also assisted the Government in achieving two "firsts," including in May 2022 facilitating the issuance of the first batch of government retail green bonds totaling HK$20 billion, which at the time represented the largest green retail bond issuance globally. In addition, we also assisted the Government in February 2023 with the issuance of the first tokenised green bonds. This represents the first globally issued tokenised green bond by a government. The issuance also marks a successful integration of our strengths in bond markets, green and sustainable finance, and financial technology, constituting a milestone achievement. Standards, data, and talent are indispensable elements for fostering the healthy development of the climate finance ecosystem, and their establishment relies on concerted efforts and collaboration across all sectors. To this end, the HKMA primarily collaborates with other relevant government departments, regulatory bodies, academic institutions, and the financial industry through a steering group to expand the aforementioned elements. In addition to the establishment of a local green taxonomy framework mentioned above, the Steering Committee has also promoted industry skills training and enhanced Hong Kong's data resources through its newly established Green and Sustainable Finance Centre. Furthermore, the Oversight Group has made significant progress in other areas, including mandatory disclosure of climate-related information and opportunities in carbon markets. In 2022, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority further strengthened the Exchange Fund's efforts in responsible investment, notably setting a target for the Exchange Fund's investment portfolio to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. At the same time, we have also optimized risk management to enhance the climate resilience of the Exchange Fund and improve risk-adjusted long-term returns. Furthermore, to fully capitalize on the opportunities presented by climate change, we are committed to advancing the sustainable investment of the Exchange Fund by identifying investment opportunities that support climate transition and climate change mitigation, thereby enhancing the long-term returns of our investment portfolio. As of the end of 2021, the weighted average carbon density of the Exchange Fund's equity portfolio had declined by 43% compared to the 2017 level. In fact, the Exchange Fund's exposure to high-carbon assets has remained lower than that of the broader market. Moving forward, we will continue to pursue our net-zero emission goals by further integrating environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors into our investment management processes, actively exercising our ownership rights, maintaining ongoing collaboration with all stakeholders, and focusing on decarbonization and transition within our investment portfolios. At the HKMA, the Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainable Development Committee, which I chair, is responsible for formulating the HKMA's sustainable development strategy. Our strategic direction is built on three pillars: environmental sustainability, employee well-being, and social responsibility. In terms of the environment, we are committed to fostering a green workplace and promoting more environmentally friendly markets to society. Regarding our employees, as a responsible and caring employer, we actively cultivate a healthy and inclusive work environment. In the realm of social responsibility, we strive to enhance the public's financial literacy, advance financial inclusion, and actively give back to the community. Compared to the baseline levels when we began tracking our carbon footprint in 2015, our per capita greenhouse gas emissions, energy consumption, and paper usage all achieved double-digit reductions by 2022. More importantly, we have established a roadmap to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050. In the short term, our goal is to fully eliminate Scope 1 emissions and reduce Scope 2 emissions by 63% from a 2015 baseline by 2030. Addressing climate change and promoting sustainable development require sustained efforts and collaboration from multiple stakeholders. On this critical global issue, we recognize the imperative to lead by example and to collaborate with like-minded industry peers and international organizations. The following section outlines the HKMA's short-term plans and key priorities for addressing climate change across its major functions. Achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 is a formidable challenge, and we are fully committed to realizing this goal. We are confident that, through the joint efforts of all our colleagues, the financial sector, and the public, we will successfully meet the climate challenges ahead. Chief Executive: Edward Yau.

In 2023, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority will continue to promote the sustainable development of Hong Kong's financial sector and uphold its responsibilities as a responsible investor and an institution committed to sustainable development. At the same time, by engaging with international and regional organizations, the HKMA is also committed to promoting the broad development and best practices of green and sustainable finance. As the banking sector's regulator, we are committed to strengthening the banking sector's climate resilience and further enhancing our green finance ecosystem to support banks' green transition. Specifically, the HKMA will engage with banks to understand their progress in implementing regulatory requirements on climate risk management, incorporating climate factors into our supervisory review processes, and revising the banking sector's "Green Benchmark" common assessment framework. At the same time, the HKMA will support banks in enhancing their climate resilience and risk management capabilities, including exploring various measures and technological solutions to assist banks in identifying, quantifying, and monitoring their climate risk exposures. The HKMA will also collaborate with banks to conduct the next round of climate risk stress testing as part of the 2023–2024 cycle of regulator-led periodic stress tests. Participating banks will be required to assess their capacity to manage climate risks in accordance with an optimized stress testing framework that encompasses multiple stress scenarios, including extreme weather events and adverse economic conditions. To foster the healthy development of banks in offering green and sustainable investment products, the Monetary Authority will closely monitor local and international market and regulatory developments, maintain communication with the industry, and provide guidance on sales processes as appropriate. We will also conduct off-site thematic assessments to gain a comprehensive understanding of the green and sustainable investment products offered by banks. At the same time, to strengthen the green finance ecosystem in support of the green transformation of the financial sector, the HKMA is planning to consult the industry on the structure and core elements of a local green taxonomy. In terms of market development, to further enhance Hong Kong's position as a regional hub for green and sustainable finance, the HKMA will assist the Government in scaling up the issuance of green bonds under the Government Green Bond Programme and broadening the programme's scope to include sustainability bonds. At the same time, through the Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme, the HKMA will attract more green financing activities to Hong Kong. The HKMA has also assisted in implementing the government-funded Green and Sustainable Finance Training Pilot Scheme to expand Hong Kong's talent pool in green finance. Furthermore, the Monetary Authority will continue to encourage more mainland local governments, institutions, and enterprises to undertake green financing through Hong Kong, and will explore the feasibility of integrating green finance with financial technology. On the other hand, we will continue to collaborate with other government agencies and sectors through the Cross-Departmental Steering Group on Green and Sustainable Finance to address cross-industry issues including skills development, data, green taxonomy, climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, as well as carbon market opportunities. Through the Green Banking Alliance, the HKMA will collaborate with the International Finance Corporation (IFC) to launch a series of regional initiatives in Asia, including green finance research, provision of distinctive market analysis, targeted professional training for banks, and practical guidance to assist banks in developing roadmaps to embed green finance as a core business. Looking ahead, the Alliance will work closely with its founding members, global partners, and knowledge partners to launch a membership program, thereby expanding its influence across Asia. At the same time, the Alliance will further enhance the professional capabilities of industry practitioners, promote the sharing of green finance knowledge, and lead the initiation of new project initiatives. As a responsible investor, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) has committed to achieving net zero emissions for its Exchange Fund portfolio by 2050 or earlier, as part of its pledge to contribute to global climate action and implement the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD). Looking ahead, the Monetary Authority of China will continue to integrate environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors into its investment management processes, strive toward net-zero emissions, and fully support global climate action. As a responsible and sustainable institution, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) is committed to the well-being of its staff, the broader community, and the surrounding environment. We have established a sustainability roadmap and set climate targets for our operations, reflecting our commitment to contribute to global decarbonization and climate action. The HKMA will continue to prioritize carbon emission reduction and encourage all staff to fully support energy conservation and waste reduction. In addition, we will provide further guidance to our employees to incorporate sustainability principles into the procurement process. To advance digital transformation and enhance operational flexibility, the HKMA will explore ways to modernize its internal systems and applications, thereby further improving efficiency while minimizing potential risks associated with the digital transformation process.

Climate change represents a significant risk to the financial system. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority has been committed to strengthening Hong Kong's financial system to build a greener and more sustainable future, contributing to Hong Kong's climate goals and the global sustainable development agenda. Banks face various impacts from sustainability and climate-related issues in their day-to-day operations. To continue fulfilling its vital role in the financial system and to channel more capital toward green and sustainable projects, banks must proactively manage climate risks. As the banking regulator, the HKMA has focused particularly on building banks' capacity to address and manage climate risks, while accelerating their efforts to support the transition to a low-carbon economy. The HKMA also supports banks in enhancing their capabilities to detect environmental crimes and has participated in the recent Hong Kong money laundering and terrorist financing risk assessment, which covers areas such as environmental crimes and illegal wildlife trafficking. In 2022, the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) issued the Principles for the Sound Management and Supervision of Climate-Related Financial Risks and issued responses to frequently asked questions, clarifying how the existing Basel framework covers these risks. In light of these global developments, the HKMA will continue to integrate climate-related factors into its regulatory framework. Following the issuance of the Supervisory Policy Manual module GS-1 "Climate Risk Management" in 2021, the HKMA continued to engage with banks to exchange views on the expectations, progress, and challenges associated with implementing the relevant regulatory requirements. To further strengthen regulatory oversight of banks' climate risk management, the HKMA has developed a two-year plan to integrate climate risk factors into the banking regulatory framework, which was communicated to the banking sector in June. As part of the implementation of the two-year plan, the HKMA issued a revised section SA-1, "Risk-Based Supervisory Framework," of the Supervisory Policy Manual, enhancing the CAMEL2 rating system by integrating climate risk into the risk-based supervisory process. At the same time, the HKMA has refined the climate risk stress test scenarios and assessment framework, drawing on lessons learned from the 2021 pilot scheme. The HKMA has also formulated a plan to incorporate the next round of climate risk stress tests into the supervisory body's regular stress testing framework, enabling a more comprehensive assessment of the banking sector's resilience under extreme climate scenarios. Under this two-year initiative, the HKMA is also enhancing its green assessment framework for banks to reflect the latest developments in sustainability-related issues, including climate risk management and transition planning. At the same time, the HKMA is reviewing the supervisory review procedures used to assess and monitor banks' capital adequacy levels and to determine their Pillar 2 capital requirements. This review aims to encourage banks to strengthen their risk management frameworks to address risks associated with climate change and the transition to carbon neutrality. Given the growing prevalence of banks issuing green and sustainable products, the HKMA conducted a thematic review, primarily examining banks' development and ongoing management of these products. During its thematic review, the HKMA identified some good practices and issued an advisory in December to share them with the industry, thereby enabling banks to progressively enhance their climate risk management capabilities. Application technologies can enhance data accessibility and strengthen banks' capacity to manage climate-related risks. The Monetary Authority has begun developing a universal platform to enable banks to assess the impact of physical risks on real estate. In addition, the HKMA, in collaboration with other central banks and regulatory authorities, has completed a project under the Innovation Network of the Bank for International Settlements to explore how technological solutions can assist in conducting physical risk assessments. The HKMA also places great emphasis on fostering sustainable and globally leading anti-money laundering practices, leveraging advanced analytics and compliance technology, complemented by fully automated regulatory data collection. Over the past 12 months, the HKMA has streamlined its anti-money laundering regulatory data collection processes to alleviate the workload and paper usage for banks. To enhance transparency across financial markets and foster greater coherence in green finance policies, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) has collaborated with other financial regulators to establish a local green taxonomy. Green classification frameworks, commonly referred to as green taxonomy, categorize economic activities as either green or sustainable, providing authorities and market participants with a reference to determine whether a given activity or its associated products are genuinely green or sustainable. To this end, the HKMA has maintained close engagement with the industry and other relevant stakeholders to thoroughly examine the framework's characteristics and challenges, and is preparing to propose and consult on the framework's structure and core elements in the first half of 2023. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority recognises that climate change may pose potential risks to the financial system; accordingly, it has expanded the scope of climate-related factors and scenarios incorporated into financial risk analysis and research to strengthen current monitoring efforts. In its ongoing monitoring of financial stability risks, the HKMA takes climate change into account and incorporates analyses of climate-related risks into its various financial stability reports. By actively participating in the Scenario Design and Analysis Working Group under the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS), the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) has helped further enrich climate scenarios, enabling central banks and regulators to better understand the impacts of climate change on the macroeconomy and the financial system. In terms of research, the HKMA conducted several applied research projects in 2022, delving into two key topics: greenwashing in the corporate green bond market and the role of disclosure in mitigating climate-related risk exposures. The findings of this study can inform the development of policies and regulatory measures to address the impact of climate risks on financial stability. Locally, these studies will help strengthen the HKMA's ongoing monitoring and assessment of the impact of climate risks on financial stability. On the external front, the HKMA has shared its research findings with various stakeholders through multiple channels, including international central bank research seminars and its semi-annual report on Monetary and Financial Stability. The HKMA's Liquidity Arrangement Framework is a secured contingent funding arrangement that provides timely liquidity support to banks in need. The HKMA is exploring the integration of sustainability considerations when assessing eligible collateral under this framework. The Monetary Authority is actively engaging in international and regional discussions on addressing climate risks and advancing sustainable finance as a mainstream agenda. Through its engagement in this area, the HKMA has helped foster international and regional policy dialogue on addressing climate change and its impact on financial stability, while drawing on insights gained to strengthen the climate resilience of Hong Kong's financial system.

To consolidate Hong Kong's position as a regional hub for green and sustainable finance, the Monetary Authority is stepping up efforts to enhance market awareness and participation, provide necessary infrastructure and catalysts, and support international initiatives to align with global standards. The Cross-Institutional Steering Group on Green and Sustainable Finance (the Steering Group), jointly led by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), is responsible for coordinating the financial sector's response to climate and environmental risks, accelerating the development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong, and supporting the Government's climate strategy. The Steering Group's work is primarily based on its strategic plan, which outlines six key priority areas and five action guidelines to strengthen Hong Kong's financial ecosystem and build a greener, more sustainable future (Figure 1). Strengthen climate-related financial risk management to consolidate Hong Kong's position as a global risk management hub; promote the flow of climate-related information across all levels to facilitate risk management, capital allocation, and investor protection; enhance the skills of industry practitioners while raising public awareness and engagement; encourage product innovation and research initiatives to channel capital toward green and sustainable projects; seize opportunities from the Mainland to develop Hong Kong as the Greater Bay Area's green finance hub; and deepen regional and international cooperation. To date, the Steering Group has made solid progress in advancing Hong Kong's sustainable finance agenda. The Steering Group's current priorities include skills training and data collection under the Green and Sustainable Finance Centre (see below), the development of a green taxonomy (see the section "Establishing a Green Taxonomy Framework to Facilitate Green Capital Flows" in Chapter 9, "Building a Sustainable Financial System"), climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, and opportunities in carbon markets. Specifically, the Steering Group announced in March its preliminary feasibility assessment of opportunities for Hong Kong's carbon market and will support Hong Kong's development as a regional carbon trading hub, including the cultivation of a high-quality international voluntary carbon market and the seizing of opportunities arising from Greater Bay Area cooperation. In December, the Steering Group announced its collaboration with CDP2 to enhance data accessibility in Hong Kong and strengthen sustainability reporting. As part of this collaboration, both parties have developed a questionnaire on climate and environmental risks targeting private companies and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). This initiative facilitates corporate sustainability reporting and assists financial institutions in collecting and analyzing company-level data for risk assessment and related business decision-making. This marks an important step by the Steering Group in expanding the scope of its data collection to include small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), a critical yet previously hard-to-reach segment of the economy. The Steering Committee established the Green and Sustainable Finance Centre in July 2021 to coordinate efforts among financial regulators, government departments, industry stakeholders, and academic institutions in training and policy formulation, and to develop resources and databases. In the first half of 2022, the Centre launched three databases focused on data, training information, and internship opportunities, facilitating access to green and sustainable finance-related data and learning resources for the financial sector and other industries. The resource centre provides data sources for assessing Hong Kong's physical risks. To support talent development in the industry, the centre assisted the Government in launching the Green and Sustainable Finance Training Pilot Programme in December, which offers subsidies to practitioners, students, and graduates participating in training and skills enhancement programmes related to green and sustainable finance. Other measures to promote skills training include launching the "Sustainable Finance Internship Programme" to create more internship opportunities for students, and introducing a new "Green and Sustainable Finance" module under the HKMA's "Banking Qualifications Framework" for banking professionals. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) has been actively supporting the development of green and sustainable finance in the region through the Green and Sustainable Finance Training Pilot Programme. In November 2020, the International Finance Corporation (IFC) and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) launched the Green Banking Alliance, bringing together financial institutions, banking industry associations, research bodies, and technology innovators from the region to jointly develop a collaborative platform for green commercial banking. The alliance aims to enable commercial banks and other financial institutions to fully realize their potential in developing green finance into a mainstream core business, while promoting the participation of the financial system in global climate change-related activities. The platform operates as a one-stop knowledge-sharing hub for financial institutions, equipping them with the necessary expertise, tools, and information to formulate their own green finance roadmaps and transform into credible green financial institutions. It brings together green finance leaders, connects green financial institutions across diverse emerging markets to foster dialogue, and addresses cutting-edge issues to advance the global green finance agenda, thereby unlocking endless green and climate-related investment opportunities. In June, five globally leading financial institutions became the founding members of the alliance and have since collaborated closely with the International Finance Corporation (IFC) and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) to encourage clients to adopt green strategies, promote best practices in green products and services, and unlock new business opportunities, all of which contribute to the transition toward a green economy. In addition, three global partners and one knowledge partner6 pledged in 2022 to provide climate expertise in areas including innovation, standardization, and academic research. Details of the alliance and its membership structure are available on the relevant webpage (in English): Founding members, the International Finance Corporation (IFC), and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU). Meanwhile, since March 2021, the alliance has held 18 training sessions and roundtable discussions, attracting over 6,000 participants from across the globe, including the Asia-Pacific region, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and the Americas. Furthermore, in June 2022, the Alliance, together with the HK Monetary and Financial Research Centre (the Centre), published its first frontier research report titled "Climate Risk: Definition, Measurement, Current Practices, and Regulation." The Monetary Authority has been promoting the issuance of green and sustainable debt and fostering a local ecosystem of related professional services. In 2022, the total amount of green and sustainable debt issued in Hong Kong (including bonds and loans) reached US$80.5 billion, a 42% increase. Green and sustainable debt issuance rose by 42% to US$80.5 billion. To demonstrate the Government's commitment to addressing climate change and to advance green finance, while striving to develop Hong Kong into a more sustainable and livable city, the Government launched the Government Green Bond Programme in 2018, with the Hong Kong Monetary Authority assisting in the issuance of green bonds under the programme. To date, the government has issued nearly USD 1.6 billion worth of green institutional and retail bonds, with proceeds allocated to over 40 green government projects, including green buildings, waste management and recycling, energy efficiency, and energy conservation. To enhance transparency and accountability, the Government publishes an annual Green Bond Report, which details the allocation of proceeds raised from green bonds and their expected environmental benefits. To enable residents to participate in Hong Kong's sustainable development through investment and share in the resulting benefits, the inaugural series of green retail bonds with a total issuance of HK$20 billion was launched in May, receiving strong public support and becoming the largest green retail bond issuance globally at the time. This issuance has also broadened the range of green and sustainable financial products in Hong Kong, further consolidating its position as a leading green finance hub in the region and internationally. The Government also continued its regular issuance of green institutional bonds in the 2022-23 financial year and issued green bonds worth US$5.75 billion in January 2023. This tri-currency issuance, covering the US dollar, euro, and renminbi, with maturities ranging from two to 30 years, continues to provide a crucial benchmark for potential issuers in Hong Kong and the broader region. The offering was warmly received by the global investment community and successfully attracted new investors who had not participated in the Government's previous green bond issuances, reflecting strong investor confidence in Hong Kong's long-term creditworthiness and economic fundamentals. In response to investor demand, the Government has doubled the issuance of Renminbi-denominated bonds to RMB 10 billion. The share allocated to international investors and to Mainland investors participating in this issuance via the Bond Connect "Southbound" channel has also increased, demonstrating Hong Kong's position as a leading offshore renminbi hub and further consolidating its leadership as an international financial centre. The HKMA also assisted the Government in issuing tokenised corporate green bonds in February 2023 to test the use of distributed ledger technology for bond issuance and settlement. This marks the first globally issued tokenised green bond by a government. This primary issuance was settled on a private blockchain network on a T+1 basis, with subsequent processes—including coupon payments, secondary market trade settlements, and redemption at maturity—also digitized. The experience gained from this government issuance can serve as a reference for market participants interested in undertaking similar bond issuances in the future. To provide the industry with credible and convenient market information, the HKMA continues to collaborate with the Climate Bonds Initiative and the International Capital Market Association to publish annual reports on the green debt markets in Hong Kong and the region. According to a report by the International Capital Market Association (ICMA), Hong Kong emerged in 2022 as the largest hub in Asia for arranging the issuance of international green and sustainable bonds, with a total volume of US$27.8 billion arranged through Hong Kong, accounting for more than one-third of the regional total. Asia emerged as the leading international hub for green and sustainable bond issuance, with a total volume of US$27.8 billion. Following its inaugural issuance in 2021, the Shenzhen Municipal People's Government re-issued RMB 5 billion in offshore local government bonds in Hong Kong in November 2022, of which RMB 2.6 billion comprised green and blue bonds. In the same month, the People's Government of Hainan Province also issued RMB 5 billion in offshore renminbi bonds in Hong Kong for the first time, comprising blue and sustainable bonds. These bond issuance activities have repeatedly highlighted Hong Kong's unique role in facilitating green and sustainable capital flows between the Mainland and the rest of the world, as well as its long-standing position as a premier fundraising platform in the region. The Monetary Authority continues to promote and implement the Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme launched in 2021, leveraging the scheme to attract more relevant professional service providers—including financial institutions, green advisory firms, and external review agencies—to establish and expand their operations in Hong Kong. The plan has been well-received by the industry. As of the end of 2022, the program has covered over 180 issuers of green and sustainable debt instruments for pre-issuance, post-issuance, or both types of external review services, helping issuers ensure and demonstrate strict adherence to market best practices and international standards. Since March, the scheme has been enhanced by lowering the minimum loan amount threshold for application of external review fee subsidies from HK$200 million to HK$100 million, thereby facilitating access to green financing for smaller enterprises. Following the successful proof-of-concept for tokenised retail green bonds under Project Genesis in 2021, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority and the HKMA Innovation Hub of the Bank for International Settlements have collaborated again under Genesis 2.0 to explore the technical feasibility of digital carbon forwards (also known as Mitigation Outcome Instruments, or MOIs), thereby enhancing transparency, objectivity, and environmental integrity in the green bond market. The project was completed in October 2022, successfully developing two prototypes that utilize blockchain and other relevant technologies to track, deliver, and transfer digital MOIs.

As one of the world's largest asset owners and managers, the Monetary Authority plays a pivotal role in advancing green and sustainable finance to support the global climate change agenda. The HKMA has also been a pioneer in responsible investing. As early as 2015, it led investments in green and sustainable assets, requiring its external investment managers to adopt the Securities and Futures Commission's Principles of Responsible Ownership and to integrate environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors into the management of the Exchange Fund's investments. In accordance with the principle of "preservation of capital first, long-term value appreciation thereafter," the HKMA invests prudently, believing that incorporating environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors can unlock long-term sustainable value and mitigate related risks. In response to the increasingly severe challenges posed by climate change, the HKMA has continued to advance its responsible investment journey, including setting a "2050 Net Zero" target in 2022 and refining its risk management strategies to enhance portfolio resilience, thereby securing more favorable risk-adjusted long-term returns for the Exchange Fund. The HKMA has also actively contributed to building a green and sustainable finance ecosystem, collaborating with like-minded investors and regulators to promote responsible investment, and working with international organizations to establish ESG investment standards. Transparency of climate-related information plays a pivotal role in managing climate risks. To fulfill its commitment to supporting the Net Zero Financial Services Alliance (NGFS) Glasgow Declaration issued at the 2021 UN Climate Change Conference and to advance the greening of the global financial system, the Monetary Authority of Hong Kong (MAHK) has prepared climate-related disclosures for the Exchange Fund in line with the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) under the Financial Stability Board (FSB). a. FCLTGlobal — Focusing Capital on the Long Term  b. PRI — Principles for Responsible Investment  c. NGFS — Network for Greening the Financial System  d. TCFD — Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures  The Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Financial Secretary, has established a framework and guiding principles for responsible investment, which are implemented by the Investment Office of the Exchange Fund in the management of the Exchange Fund's investments. The primary guiding principle is to prioritize ESG investments that deliver risk-adjusted long-term returns comparable to other asset classes, thereby aligning with the Exchange Fund's investment objectives. Details of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's (HKMA) Responsible Investment Framework are available on the HKMA website: The Investment Committee, established under the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee and chaired by the HKMA Chief Executive, is responsible for overseeing environmental, social, and governance (ESG) and climate-related risks associated with Exchange Fund investments. The Investment Committee reviews the Responsible Investment Framework and Risk Management Guidelines, and monitors the progress of integrating ESG factors into investments and the Exchange Fund's ESG status through regular reporting from the Risk Management and Oversight Division of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. As illustrated in Figure 1, the ESG Committee under the Exchange Fund Investment Office is chaired by the Chief Risk Officer and is responsible for coordinating and overseeing all ESG-related activities of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. The motions discussed and progress of work at each meeting of the ESG Committee are reported to the Chief Executive of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. The governance framework for responsible investing, together with the dedicated task force of the Risk Management and Monitoring Department, collaborates closely with the investment teams of the Exchange Fund Investment Office to integrate ESG factors and assist senior management in managing ESG and climate-related risks and opportunities across various investment portfolios. For public market investments, the Credit, Regulatory and Monitoring Committee, composed of senior management of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, monitors the ESG profile of fixed-income portfolios through regular reporting from the Risk Management and Monitoring Department. In addition, the Risk Management and Monitoring Department also participates in the selection, appointment, and oversight process of external investment managers for equity portfolios from an ESG perspective (see the section "Proactive Exercise of Ownership Rights" under "Risk Management" on page 27). Private Market Investments: The Investment Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the Monetary Authority, will consider the ESG-related assessments provided by the Risk Management and Surveillance Department and the Private Market Investment team for each investment proposal. Specific evidence² continues to indicate that the impacts of climate change and associated risks remain significant. According to the latest report of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), even if all nationally determined contributions (NDCs) announced by countries are fully implemented, global temperature rise is projected to reach 2.1°C to 2.4°C by 2100, making it unlikely to achieve the Paris Agreement's goal of limiting global average temperature increase to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels. If regions adopt more ambitious policy measures to narrow temperature gaps, the associated transition risks⁴, market-driven repricing of assets based on anticipated future trends, and inherent physical risks will collectively intensify pressure on asset valuations. In light of updated global warming trajectories and model assumptions, the HKMA leveraged the expertise of external consultants to further assess the resilience of the Exchange Fund's investment portfolio under a "rapid transition" scenario (Figure 2), building upon the scenarios evaluated in 2021. The "rapid transition" scenario incorporates elevated transition risk factors in the short, medium, and long terms, assuming that policy changes and technological advancements jointly drive a swift decline in carbon emissions, while a wide range of assets are abruptly divested to keep global average temperature rise below 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels by 2100. The scenarios are broadly consistent with the disorderly scenario recommended by the NGFS for forward-looking climate impact assessments. The portfolio is expected to remain resilient over the medium to long term, as a significant portion of its asset allocation consists of sovereign bonds that are less sensitive to transition-related impacts. Industry distribution is key. Low-carbon power and renewable energy assets stand to benefit from the ongoing transition. Transition risks and the repricing of assets may impact performance in the short term, particularly for equity assets. The portfolio as a whole will be increasingly affected by physical risks that gradually materialize over time. Energy and traditional utilities remain the sectors most vulnerable to such developments. Climate scenario analysis, like other modeling approaches, has its own limitations. The analysis is based on strategic asset allocation with benchmark industry allocations and does not account for the impact of actively selecting specific securities within an industry. Deeper research reveals that investment items within portfolios generally demonstrate greater resilience to transition shocks or suffer less severe impacts compared to market benchmarks under strategic asset allocation. This result further affirms that the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's focus on responsible investment to counter climate change can enhance portfolio resilience. The trajectory of climate change remains uncertain, and scenario analysis will continue to evolve as data quality improves and policies develop. The HKMA will regularly review relevant scenarios and enhance assessments to more clearly confirm the resilience of the Exchange Fund in the face of climate change. As a long-term investor, the HKMA fully recognises the risks and opportunities associated with climate change. The Monetary Authority is committed to further expanding sustainable investment and capitalizing on opportunities related to climate transition, climate risk mitigation, and enhancing long-term portfolio returns. In 2022, the Monetary Authority maintained its strong momentum, increasing its holdings of green, social, and sustainability bonds by a further 50%. In equity investments, the Monetary Authority of Hong Kong (MAHK) invests in actively managed equity portfolios with a governance focus and adopts a low-carbon strategy for passive equity portfolios, tilting them toward companies with lower carbon emissions. Furthermore, the Monetary Authority is working with the specialist partners of the Exchange Fund's Long-Term Growth Portfolio to explore the establishment of a dedicated private equity fund aimed at advancing green and sustainable development in Asia (Figure 3). Figure 3: Continuing measures to promote ESG investment. The Monetary Authority has invested in a pan-African wind power operator that, in addition to generating clean energy, places strong emphasis on social factors and biodiversity conservation. Before the establishment of wind farms, local villagers used poisoned baits to prevent predators from attacking their livestock, but this inadvertently endangered certain vulture species that are critically endangered. Livestock constitute a vital asset for local villagers. To assist villagers in safeguarding their livestock, the operator has constructed livestock shelters within the wind farm to protect the animals from predation by wild animals. Additionally, operators employ bird monitoring teams that issue warnings when vultures are attracted to animal carcasses left by predators, prompting the immediate shutdown of wind turbines to prevent birds from being struck by the blades. Reducing livestock predation creates a win-win situation: it safeguards villagers' livelihoods while simultaneously lowering the number of vultains killed by wind turbines, thereby protecting endangered species. Sound ESG practices can generate new business opportunities and expand revenue streams for enterprises, as illustrated by the following supply chain-related operations. The investee company is a comprehensive logistics and warehousing operator based in mainland China, specializing in cold chain logistics for pharmaceuticals, chemical products, and high-end consumer goods. The company faces increasingly stringent ESG operational standards, primarily driven by its multinational corporate clients requiring its service providers to meet high decarbonization targets aligned with the Paris Agreement. In response to this need, the company engaged external consultants to develop a "Three-Year ESG Plan" aiming to reduce carbon emission intensity by 50% by 2030 or earlier. This comprehensive decarbonization plan has already yielded significant results in 2021 alone. These ESG measures enabled the company to receive the "Low-Carbon Green Management Case" award from the China Federation of Logistics & Purchasing. These achievements and accolades have enabled the company to secure numerous business opportunities with multinational consumer and chemical product clients that place particular emphasis on ESG practices. The growth of ESG investment is closely linked to the development of the green and sustainable finance ecosystem. The HKMA actively collaborates with like-minded investors and partners to promote responsible investment and enhance industry skills. In 2022, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority successfully hosted its fourth annual ESG workshop, engaging nine participating private market institutions—including general partners, limited partners, and corporate entities—to exchange best practices in ESG and promote sustainable investment opportunities across the Asia-Pacific region and the Greater Bay Area. In the open market, the Monetary Authority has urged trading partners, primarily investment banks, to expand their ESG staffing and research capabilities, particularly in Hong Kong. In his opening remarks at the 2022 HKMA ESG Workshop, Mr. Li Tat-ji, Chief Executive of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, highlighted the HKMA's active role at the international level in developing industry standards and practices for ESG investment. As one of the earliest central bank signatories to the Principles for Responsible Investment (PRI), the HKMA has participated in joint initiatives coordinated by the PRI to develop a harmonized responsible investment due diligence questionnaire for private equity and venture capital investments. This questionnaire aims to assist private market investors in conducting ESG assessments of dedicated partners and investment recommendations. The HKMA has participated in several working groups to support the research conducted by FCLTGlobal, which aims to examine leading market practices for long-term portfolios and decarbonizing private assets, as well as the applicability of these practices for long-term investors. As a member of the NGFS and a supporter of the TCFD, the HKMA contributed to the NGFS's "Central Bank Climate-related Disclosure Guidelines," demonstrating its commitment to adopting best practices in ESG. The HKMA also led a working group under the Net-Zero Banking Alliance (NGFS) "Central Bank Net-Zero" initiative to help develop sustainable and responsible investment guidelines for the central banking community. The Monetary Authority continues to actively participate in various industry forums and seminars, sharing insights on responsible investment and climate change strategies. Ms. Laura Lau, Chief Risk Officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, delivered a speech at the ESG investment opportunities sharing session. Building internal capabilities is crucial for continuing the ESG journey. In addition to encouraging staff to pursue courses and obtain qualifications related to sustainable development, the HKMA has also drawn on relevant knowledge and practical experience from the 2021 engagement of external consultants on leading industry practices for climate transition within investment portfolios. On the other hand, the HKMA utilizes ESG data compiled by reputable third-party information providers to supplement its ongoing portfolio analysis, thereby strengthening the resilience of the Exchange Fund in relation to ESG considerations.

The HKMA is committed to reducing its own institutional carbon footprint, aiming to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 or sooner, thereby contributing to Hong Kong's overall climate goals. On one hand, the Monetary Authority strives to advance environmental sustainability; on the other, it upholds its commitment to caring for employees' physical and mental well-being, promoting financial inclusion, and fulfilling its social responsibilities. The HKMA is committed to carrying out its day-to-day operations in a responsible and sustainable manner. To this end, the HKMA has put into practice the concept of sustainable development under three pillars: environment, employees, and social responsibility (Figure 1). The Committee on Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainable Development is responsible for leading the HKMA in formulating and implementing sustainable development strategies. The Committee is chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA and includes three Deputy Chief Executives as well as representatives from the Risk Management and Surveillance Department and the Institutional Development and Operations Department; it submits regular reports to the Governance Committee under the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee. Under the leadership of this Committee, multiple teams and working groups have been tasked with planning and implementing measures within their respective areas of responsibility. In 2022, the Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee approved the institution's climate objectives and reviewed its transition roadmap to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. Throughout the year, the Committee continued to review the progress of the HKMA's green initiatives, including proposals to strengthen the HKMA's sustainable procurement policies, procedures, and methodologies. A sustainable governance framework. The HKMA's journey in corporate sustainability has been recognized for its commitment to caring for the environment, employees, and society as a whole. For the 16th consecutive year, the Hong Kong Council of Social Service has awarded the HKMA the "15+ Years of Caring with One Heart" mark. The HKMA is highly concerned about its own carbon footprint and has developed internal "Green Office Guidelines" to manage the environmental impact of its operational processes. The HKMA has integrated environmental considerations into the interior design, operations, and maintenance of its offices. In 2022, the BEAM Plus scheme awarded a Gold certification to the Hong Kong Monetary Authority for certain renovated office areas. This is the second green building certification obtained after achieving LEED Gold certification in 2021. The project was awarded the Green Building Council's BEAM Plus Indoor Environment Version 1.0 Gold certification, while the Hong Kong Monetary Authority has implemented a range of energy-saving measures. Total energy consumption in 2022 was 4,996.4 megawatt-hours (2.8 megawatt-hours per person), a 24.4% decrease from 2015 (Figure 1). Total Scope 1 and Scope 2 greenhouse gas emissions in 2022 were 2,996.4 metric tons of CO2 equivalent (tCO2e) (1.7 tCO2e per capita), representing a 38.2% decrease from 2015 levels (Figure 2).
